name: Alveoli
shortExplanation: The tiny air sacs at the end of the airways where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.

sections.purpose: Provide the vast, thin surface where oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. A film of surfactant keeps the alveoli open by lowering surface tension.
sections.careConsiderations: Alveolar disease impairs gas exchange: fluid (pulmonary edema, ARDS), infection (pneumonia), or collapse (atelectasis) cause hypoxemia. Nurses use incentive spirometry, positioning, and early mobility to keep alveoli open, and surfactant deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

name: Cardiac Conduction System
shortExplanation: The heart's built-in electrical wiring that sets the beat — starting at the SA node and traveling through the AV node to the ventricles.

sections.purpose: Generate and coordinate each heartbeat. The SA node (natural pacemaker) fires, the impulse pauses at the AV node to let the ventricles fill, then travels down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to contract the ventricles.
sections.careConsiderations: Where the signal fails maps to the arrhythmia: SA node problems cause bradycardia; AV node/His block causes heart block; abnormal ventricular foci cause VT/VF. This system is the target of pacemakers, ablation, and rate/rhythm drugs.

name: Cerebral Lobes
shortExplanation: The four lobes of the cerebrum - frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital - each with distinct functions.

sections.purpose: Divide the cerebrum by function: the frontal lobe governs movement, judgment, and personality; the parietal lobe processes sensation and spatial awareness; the temporal lobe handles hearing, language, and memory; and the occipital lobe processes vision.
sections.careConsiderations: Localizing deficits helps interpret strokes and injuries - for example, frontal changes in behavior, temporal language deficits (aphasia), or occipital visual field loss. Nurses perform focused neuro checks and note new deficits, which guide stroke recognition and management.

name: Coronary Arteries
shortExplanation: The vessels that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen-rich blood — the ones that get blocked in a heart attack.

sections.purpose: Deliver oxygenated blood to the myocardium. The left main branches into the LAD (anterior wall) and circumflex (lateral wall); the right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes.
sections.careConsiderations: ECG lead groupings map to territories (inferior II/III/aVF ≈ RCA; anterior V1–V4 ≈ LAD; lateral I/aVL/V5–V6 ≈ circumflex), which helps localize an infarct; RCA involvement often causes bradycardia and heart block.

name: Gastrointestinal Tract
shortExplanation: The digestive tube running from mouth to anus that breaks down food, absorbs nutrients, and eliminates waste.

sections.purpose: Digests food and absorbs nutrients and water. It includes the esophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), and large intestine, supported by the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.
sections.careConsiderations: GI problems are common on every unit: bleeding, obstruction, ileus, and impaired absorption. Nurses assess bowel sounds, distension, nausea, and stool, verify feeding-tube placement, and monitor for GI bleeding (melena, hematemesis) and the return of bowel function after surgery.

name: Heart Chambers
shortExplanation: The heart's four rooms — two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it — working as a right and left pump in series.

sections.purpose: Move blood through the body. The right atrium and ventricle receive deoxygenated blood and pump it to the lungs; the left atrium and ventricle receive oxygenated blood and pump it to the body — the left ventricle does the hardest work.
sections.careConsiderations: Right-sided failure shows as systemic congestion (JVD, peripheral edema); left-sided failure shows as pulmonary congestion (crackles, dyspnea); the left ventricle's function is summarized by the ejection fraction.

name: Heart Valves
shortExplanation: The four one-way valves that keep blood moving in the right direction through the heart — the mitral, tricuspid, aortic, and pulmonic valves.

sections.purpose: Prevent backflow as the heart pumps. The tricuspid and mitral (AV) valves sit between atria and ventricles; the pulmonic and aortic (semilunar) valves guard the outflow to the lungs and body.
sections.careConsiderations: Valves can narrow (stenosis) or leak (regurgitation), each producing a characteristic murmur; severe disease is treated with repair or replacement (surgical or transcatheter, e.g. TAVR); prosthetic valves often require anticoagulation and raise endocarditis risk.

name: Meninges
shortExplanation: The three protective membranes (dura, arachnoid, and pia mater) that surround the brain and spinal cord.

sections.purpose: Protect and support the brain and spinal cord and contain the cerebrospinal fluid that cushions them. The layers, from outer to inner, are the dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater.
sections.careConsiderations: The meninges are clinically central to lumbar puncture (the needle passes into the subarachnoid space to sample CSF) and to bleeds named by layer (epidural, subdural, subarachnoid). Infection of the meninges is meningitis - watch for fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.

name: Nephron
shortExplanation: The microscopic filtering unit of the kidney; each kidney has about a million of them.

sections.purpose: Filters blood and forms urine. The glomerulus filters plasma, and the tubules reabsorb water, electrolytes, and nutrients while secreting wastes, regulating fluid balance, blood pressure, acid-base status, and electrolytes.
sections.careConsiderations: Nephron injury underlies acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease. Because nephrons are damaged by low perfusion, nephrotoxic drugs, and obstruction, nurses monitor urine output, creatinine, and BUN and use caution with contrast and nephrotoxins.

name: Acute Agitation
shortExplanation: A state of severe restlessness, distress, or aggression that can pose a safety risk to the patient and others and needs prompt, calm management.

sections.presentation: Escalating motor restlessness, loud or threatening speech, pacing, clenched fists, and hostility, which may stem from psychiatric illness, intoxication or withdrawal, delirium, or a medical cause.
sections.typicalTreatments: Begin with verbal de-escalation and a safe, low-stimulation environment. Look for and treat underlying medical causes such as hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or infection. Medications (benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics) are used when behavioral measures are insufficient, with physical restraint reserved as a last resort with close monitoring.
sections.riskFactors: Psychosis, mania, substance intoxication or withdrawal, delirium and dementia, and untreated pain or metabolic derangements.

name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
shortExplanation: A blocked or critically narrowed coronary artery starving heart muscle of oxygen — the umbrella term for unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI (heart attack).

sections.presentation: Chest pressure or pain (often radiating to the arm/jaw), shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea; women, older adults, and diabetics may present atypically.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aspirin plus a second antiplatelet, anticoagulation, nitroglycerin, oxygen if hypoxic, statin; emergent cardiac catheterization (PCI) for STEMI; serial troponins and ECGs.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, family history, older age, obesity.

name: Acute Ischemic Stroke
shortExplanation: A blocked artery cuts off blood flow to part of the brain, causing sudden neurologic deficits. Rapid treatment can save brain tissue.

sections.presentation: Sudden face droop, arm or leg weakness (often one-sided), slurred or garbled speech, vision changes, severe imbalance, or confusion. Time of last known well is critical.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent non-contrast CT to rule out bleeding, IV thrombolytics (such as alteplase or tenecteplase) within the treatment window, and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion. Careful blood pressure management, glucose control, and swallow screening before oral intake.
sections.riskFactors: Atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, prior stroke or TIA, and older age.

name: Acute Kidney Injury
shortExplanation: A sudden drop in kidney function over hours to days, shown by rising creatinine and/or falling urine output, common in critically ill patients.

sections.presentation: Decreased urine output, rising creatinine and BUN, fluid overload, and electrolyte disturbances such as hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. Often detected on labs before symptoms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the cause, restore perfusion and volume, stop or dose-adjust nephrotoxic drugs, and manage electrolytes and fluid balance. Dialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy for severe or refractory cases.
sections.riskFactors: Hypotension or shock, sepsis, nephrotoxic medications, contrast exposure, major surgery, heart failure, and pre-existing kidney disease.

name: Acute Liver Failure
shortExplanation: Rapid loss of liver function in a person without prior liver disease, causing coagulopathy and confusion. A medical emergency, often from acetaminophen overdose.

sections.presentation: Jaundice, confusion (hepatic encephalopathy), coagulopathy with easy bleeding, nausea, and right upper quadrant discomfort developing over days to weeks. Can progress to cerebral edema, multi-organ failure, and hypoglycemia.
sections.typicalTreatments: ICU care with treatment of the cause (N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity), management of cerebral edema and coagulopathy, glucose monitoring, and early transfer to a transplant center. Emergency liver transplant may be lifesaving.
sections.riskFactors: Acetaminophen overdose, viral hepatitis, drug reactions, autoimmune hepatitis, and ischemia (shock liver).

name: Acute Pancreatitis
shortExplanation: Sudden inflammation of the pancreas, most often from gallstones or alcohol. Ranges from mild and self-limited to severe with organ failure.

sections.presentation: Severe, steady epigastric pain that radiates to the back, nausea and vomiting, and abdominal tenderness. Fever, tachycardia, and hypotension in severe disease. Elevated lipase (and amylase). Rare bruising around the flanks (Grey Turner) or umbilicus (Cullen) signals hemorrhagic disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, pain control, antiemetics, and bowel rest with early feeding as tolerated. Treat the cause (gallstone removal via ERCP, alcohol cessation). Monitor for complications: necrosis, pseudocyst, and organ failure.
sections.riskFactors: Gallstones, heavy alcohol use, high triglycerides, certain medications, ERCP, and hypercalcemia.

name: Acute Pulmonary Edema
shortExplanation: Sudden fluid accumulation in the alveoli, most often from acute heart failure, causing severe shortness of breath and hypoxemia.

sections.presentation: Acute severe dyspnea, orthopnea, restlessness, pink frothy sputum, diffuse crackles, tachypnea, tachycardia, and low oxygen saturation. Patients often sit upright and appear anxious/diaphoretic.
sections.typicalTreatments: Sit upright, high-flow oxygen or noninvasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP), IV loop diuretics (furosemide), nitroglycerin for preload reduction, and treatment of the underlying cardiac cause. Intubation if refractory.
sections.riskFactors: Heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, severe hypertension, valvular disease, arrhythmia, and volume overload (including renal failure).

name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
shortExplanation: Sudden, severe lung inflammation that floods the air sacs with fluid, causing dangerously low oxygen levels that often require a ventilator.

sections.presentation: Rapidly worsening shortness of breath and low oxygen levels not explained by heart failure, with diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging, usually within a week of a known insult such as pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, or trauma.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause; lung-protective mechanical ventilation using low tidal volumes; prone positioning for severe cases; careful fluid management; and sedation with or without paralysis as needed.
sections.riskFactors: Sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, severe trauma, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, and inhalation injury.

name: Acute Respiratory Failure
shortExplanation: The lungs suddenly cannot get enough oxygen into the blood (hypoxemic) or clear enough carbon dioxide (hypercapnic), a common reason for ICU admission and intubation.

sections.presentation: Shortness of breath, rapid or labored breathing, use of accessory muscles, restlessness or confusion, and low oxygen saturation. Rising carbon dioxide can cause drowsiness. An arterial blood gas confirms the type and severity.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supplemental oxygen, treating the underlying cause, noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) for selected patients, and intubation with mechanical ventilation when these fail or the airway is at risk.
sections.riskFactors: COPD, pneumonia, heart failure, asthma, ARDS, neuromuscular weakness, opioid overdose, and chest wall or airway problems.

name: Adrenal Insufficiency (Addisonian Crisis)
shortExplanation: A condition in which the adrenal glands produce too little cortisol (and sometimes aldosterone). An acute crisis causes life-threatening low blood pressure.

sections.presentation: Chronic: fatigue, weakness, weight loss, low appetite, salt craving, and skin darkening (in primary disease). Acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis: severe hypotension and shock, abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia, often triggered by illness or stress.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate IV hydrocortisone (stress-dose steroids) and aggressive IV fluids with dextrose for crisis; treat the precipitant. Chronic disease is managed with daily glucocorticoid (and mineralocorticoid in primary disease) replacement. Patients need stress dosing during illness and a medical alert identification.
sections.riskFactors: Autoimmune adrenal destruction, abrupt withdrawal of long-term steroids, pituitary disease, and physiologic stress (infection, surgery) in a person with limited adrenal reserve.

name: Alcohol Withdrawal
shortExplanation: The set of symptoms that appear when a person dependent on alcohol suddenly stops or reduces drinking, which can become life-threatening.

sections.presentation: Tremor, anxiety, agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension begin within hours. More severe stages include hallucinations, withdrawal seizures, and delirium tremens, which features confusion, severe autonomic instability, and can be fatal.
sections.typicalTreatments: Benzodiazepines are the mainstay, often dosed using a symptom-triggered approach guided by the CIWA-Ar scale. Add thiamine (before glucose) to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, along with IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and a calm monitored environment.
sections.riskFactors: Long-term heavy alcohol use, prior withdrawal episodes or seizures, prior delirium tremens, and abrupt cessation.

name: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
shortExplanation: The set of symptoms that appear when a person who drinks heavily suddenly stops, ranging from tremors and anxiety to seizures and life-threatening delirium tremens.

sections.presentation: Tremors, anxiety, sweating, fast heart rate, hypertension, nausea, and insomnia within hours to days of the last drink. Severe cases progress to hallucinations, seizures, and delirium tremens (confusion, agitation, fever, and autonomic instability).
sections.typicalTreatments: Benzodiazepines titrated to symptoms (often using a scoring tool such as CIWA-Ar), a calm and monitored environment, IV fluids, thiamine before glucose, and correction of electrolytes (magnesium, potassium, phosphorus). ICU care for severe delirium tremens.
sections.riskFactors: Long-standing heavy alcohol use, prior withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, and abrupt cessation, often during hospitalization for another reason.

name: Alzheimer Disease and Dementia
shortExplanation: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia, marked by gradual decline in memory, thinking, and function.

sections.presentation: Insidious, progressive memory loss (especially recent events), word-finding difficulty, impaired judgment and problem-solving, disorientation, and later loss of ability to perform daily activities. Behavioral and psychological symptoms and agitation are common in later stages.
sections.typicalTreatments: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine may modestly help symptoms; structured routines, safety measures, and caregiver support; nonpharmacologic strategies for behavioral symptoms; treat superimposed delirium and reversible contributors.
sections.riskFactors: Advancing age, family history and genetics (including APOE), cardiovascular risk factors, head injury, low physical and cognitive activity.

name: Aortic Stenosis
shortExplanation: The aortic valve narrows and stiffens, forcing the heart to work harder to push blood out — leading to chest pain, fainting, and heart failure as it worsens.

sections.presentation: Exertional chest pain, syncope, and dyspnea; a harsh systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids; narrowed pulse pressure in severe disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Valve replacement when symptomatic or severe — surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVR); careful management of blood pressure and volume; avoid abrupt vasodilation.
sections.riskFactors: Older age (calcific degeneration), bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic heart disease, chronic kidney disease.

name: Apnea of Prematurity
shortExplanation: Pauses in breathing in premature infants caused by an immature respiratory control center in the brain.

sections.presentation: Breathing pauses, often lasting 20 seconds or longer or shorter pauses accompanied by a slow heart rate or drop in oxygen saturation, in a preterm infant.
sections.typicalTreatments: Gentle stimulation, caffeine to stimulate the respiratory center, and respiratory support such as CPAP when needed. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is essential, and new or worsening apnea should prompt evaluation for infection or other causes.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity (more frequent the earlier the gestational age); apnea may also be worsened by infection, anemia, or reflux.

name: Appendicitis
shortExplanation: Inflammation of the appendix, usually from obstruction, that can progress to rupture. A common surgical emergency.

sections.presentation: Pain that begins near the umbilicus and migrates to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point), anorexia, nausea, low-grade fever, and rebound tenderness. Sudden relief followed by worsening diffuse pain suggests rupture and peritonitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Appendectomy is standard; antibiotics are given and, in selected uncomplicated cases, may be used alone. IV fluids, pain control, and NPO status while awaiting surgery. Avoid applying heat or laxatives, which may promote rupture.
sections.riskFactors: Most common between the ages of 10 and 30, but can occur at any age.

name: Ascites
shortExplanation: Buildup of fluid in the abdominal cavity, most often from cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Large volumes cause distension and breathing difficulty.

sections.presentation: Abdominal distension and discomfort, weight gain, a fluid wave or shifting dullness on exam, and early satiety. Large ascites can cause shortness of breath. Fever and abdominal pain raise concern for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Sodium restriction and diuretics (typically spironolactone with furosemide), therapeutic paracentesis for large or tense ascites, and albumin replacement after large-volume taps. Treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with antibiotics. Monitor daily weights and abdominal girth.
sections.riskFactors: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension, heart failure, malignancy, and kidney disease.

name: Aspiration Pneumonia
shortExplanation: Lung infection or inflammation that develops after inhaling food, stomach contents, or secretions into the airways, common in patients with impaired swallowing or reduced consciousness.

sections.presentation: Cough, fever, shortness of breath, low oxygen, and purulent sputum, often after a witnessed aspiration event or in a patient at risk. Infiltrates typically appear in dependent lung regions.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supplemental oxygen and airway support, suctioning, and antibiotics guided by severity and risk. Supportive care and treatment of respiratory failure as needed. Swallow evaluation and aspiration precautions to prevent recurrence.
sections.riskFactors: Impaired swallowing, stroke, decreased consciousness, sedation, tube feeding, gastroesophageal reflux, and intubation or extubation.

name: Asthma
shortExplanation: A chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible bronchospasm, causing episodic wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath triggered by allergens, exercise, or irritants.

sections.presentation: Wheezing, chest tightness, dry cough (often nocturnal), prolonged expiration, and dyspnea. Severe attacks show accessory muscle use, inability to speak full sentences, and a silent chest with low peak flow.
sections.typicalTreatments: Short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol) for rescue; inhaled corticosteroids for control, often combined with long-acting beta-agonists; leukotriene modifiers (montelukast) and systemic steroids for exacerbations. Trigger avoidance and an asthma action plan.
sections.riskFactors: Atopy/allergies, family history, eczema, tobacco or air-pollution exposure, obesity, and viral respiratory infections.

name: Atrial Fibrillation
shortExplanation: An irregular, often rapid heart rhythm originating in the atria that increases the risk of stroke and can reduce the heart's pumping efficiency.

sections.presentation: Irregularly irregular pulse, palpitations, fatigue, sometimes asymptomatic and found incidentally on telemetry.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate control (beta-blockers, amiodarone), rhythm control (antiarrhythmics, cardioversion), anticoagulation (warfarin or other agents) to reduce stroke risk.
sections.riskFactors: Advanced age, hypertension, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, excessive alcohol use.

name: Bacterial Meningitis
shortExplanation: Inflammation of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord caused by bacterial infection. It is a medical emergency that can rapidly become fatal.

sections.presentation: Classic triad of fever, headache, and neck stiffness; also photophobia, altered mental status, nausea, seizures, and petechial or purpuric rash (meningococcal). Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Infants may show poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, and irritability.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent empiric IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone plus vancomycin) started immediately, ideally after blood cultures without delaying treatment; lumbar puncture for CSF analysis; adjunctive dexamethasone in certain cases; droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective therapy for suspected meningococcal disease.
sections.riskFactors: Recent respiratory or ear infection, close-quarters living, immunocompromise, absent or nonfunctioning spleen, missing vaccinations, age extremes, CSF leak or neurosurgery.

name: Bell Palsy
shortExplanation: Sudden weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face from dysfunction of the facial nerve. Most cases recover over weeks to months.

sections.presentation: Rapid-onset unilateral facial droop involving the forehead (unable to raise the eyebrow or close the eye on the affected side), loss of the nasolabial fold, drooling, altered taste, and sensitivity to sound. Forehead involvement helps distinguish it from stroke.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral corticosteroids started early; antivirals may be added in some cases; eye protection is essential (lubricating drops, taping the eye at night) because the eye may not close fully; most patients recover.
sections.riskFactors: Recent viral illness, pregnancy, diabetes, and possible reactivation of herpes simplex virus.

name: Bronchiolitis
shortExplanation: A common lower respiratory infection in infants, most often from RSV, that inflames the small airways and causes wheezing and difficulty breathing.

sections.presentation: Begins with runny nose and cough, then progresses to wheezing, tachypnea, nasal flaring, retractions, and feeding difficulty in a child under 2 years. Apnea can occur in young infants.
sections.typicalTreatments: Mainly supportive: nasal suctioning to clear secretions, adequate hydration, and supplemental oxygen for low saturations. Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely effective. Monitor respiratory status and hydration closely.
sections.riskFactors: Age under 2 years (especially under 6 months), prematurity, RSV season, secondhand smoke exposure, and daycare attendance.

name: Cardiac Arrest
shortExplanation: The heart abruptly stops pumping effectively, so blood flow to the brain and body ceases — reversible only with immediate CPR and ACLS.

sections.presentation: Sudden unresponsiveness, no pulse, and no normal breathing (or only gasping). Underlying rhythm may be shockable (VF/pulseless VT) or non-shockable (asystole/PEA).
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate high-quality CPR, defibrillation for shockable rhythms, epinephrine per ACLS, advanced airway, and identifying/treating reversible causes (the Hs and Ts).
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease/MI, heart failure, severe electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, drug overdose, prior arrest.

name: Cardiac Tamponade
shortExplanation: Fluid building up in the sac around the heart squeezes it so it can't fill properly — a life-threatening emergency that drops blood pressure fast.

sections.presentation: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins), pulsus paradoxus, tachycardia, dyspnea, low-voltage ECG or electrical alternans.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage, IV fluids as a temporizing measure to support filling, treat the underlying cause.
sections.riskFactors: Pericarditis, chest trauma, recent cardiac procedure, malignancy, aortic dissection, post-MI wall rupture.

name: Cardiogenic Shock
shortExplanation: The heart is too weak to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs — organs start to fail from poor perfusion. Most often follows a large heart attack.

sections.presentation: Hypotension, cool/mottled extremities, weak pulses, altered mental status, low urine output, pulmonary congestion, rising lactate.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the cause (e.g. urgent revascularization for MI), inotropes (dobutamine), vasopressors, and mechanical support such as an intra-aortic balloon pump in severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Large myocardial infarction, advanced heart failure, severe arrhythmia, acute valve failure.

name: Catheter-Associated UTI
shortExplanation: A urinary tract infection linked to an indwelling urinary catheter. It is a common, largely preventable healthcare-associated infection.

sections.presentation: New fever, suprapubic or flank pain or tenderness, and change in urine appearance or character in a catheterized patient, often with few localized symptoms; altered mental status may be the only sign in older adults. Diagnosis requires symptoms plus a positive urine culture, not merely cloudy urine or asymptomatic bacteriuria.
sections.typicalTreatments: Remove or replace the catheter when possible; antibiotics guided by urine culture; avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. Prevention centers on inserting catheters only when indicated, sterile insertion, maintaining a closed system, and removing them as early as possible.
sections.riskFactors: Prolonged catheterization, breaks in the closed drainage system, poor insertion technique, female sex, older age, diabetes, and immobility.

name: Cellulitis
shortExplanation: A bacterial infection of the skin and underlying tissue that causes a spreading area of redness, warmth, and swelling.

sections.presentation: Warm, red, swollen, tender skin with poorly defined borders, most often on a lower leg; may have fever, chills, and red streaking toward lymph nodes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics targeting skin bacteria, limb elevation, marking the border of redness to track spread, and pain control.
sections.riskFactors: Breaks in the skin, edema and venous insufficiency, diabetes, obesity, and lymphedema.

name: Central-Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection
shortExplanation: A serious bloodstream infection that develops in a patient with a central venous catheter and is not from another source. It is largely preventable with proper line care.

sections.presentation: Fever and chills, and possibly hypotension or signs of sepsis; the catheter exit site may show redness, tenderness, or purulence. Confirmed with blood cultures, ideally drawn from the catheter and a peripheral site.
sections.typicalTreatments: Blood cultures then prompt empiric IV antibiotics (often covering MRSA) adjusted to culture results; consider removing the catheter, especially with instability or certain organisms; source control. Prevention uses insertion bundles, chlorhexidine skin prep, maximal sterile barriers, daily necessity review, and scrupulous hub disinfection.
sections.riskFactors: Prolonged catheter dwell time, femoral or multiple-lumen access, frequent line access, parenteral nutrition, immunocompromise, and breaks in sterile technique.

name: Chemotherapy Extravasation
shortExplanation: The accidental leakage of chemotherapy from the vein into surrounding tissue during infusion. With vesicant drugs this can cause severe pain, blistering, and tissue death.

sections.presentation: Burning or pain, swelling, redness, and lack of blood return at the IV site during or after infusion. Vesicant extravasation can progress over days to blistering, ulceration, and necrosis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the infusion immediately while leaving the catheter in place to aspirate residual drug, then remove it and elevate the limb. Apply cold or warm compresses and give a specific antidote depending on the drug, mark and photograph the area, and involve the provider and pharmacy; surgery may be needed for severe injury.
sections.riskFactors: Vesicant drugs such as anthracyclines and vinca alkaloids, small or fragile peripheral veins, poor catheter placement, patient movement, and infusing vesicants peripherally rather than through a central line or port.

name: CHF Exacerbation
shortExplanation: Acute worsening of heart failure symptoms, often from fluid overload.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles on lung auscultation, jugular venous distension, peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Loop diuretics (furosemide), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, fluid and sodium restriction.
sections.riskFactors: Prior heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension, medication/dietary non-adherence.

name: Cholecystitis
shortExplanation: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from a gallstone blocking the cystic duct. Causes right upper quadrant pain and can become infected.

sections.presentation: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, often after fatty meals, that may radiate to the right shoulder. Nausea, vomiting, fever, and a positive Murphy sign (pain and arrest of inspiration on palpation under the right costal margin).
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest, IV fluids, pain control, antiemetics, and antibiotics for infection. Cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment; a cholecystostomy tube may be used in poor surgical candidates.
sections.riskFactors: Gallstones, female sex, obesity, pregnancy, rapid weight loss, and age over 40.

name: Chronic Kidney Disease
shortExplanation: A gradual, long-term loss of kidney function; at its end stage (ESRD) it requires dialysis or a transplant.

sections.presentation: Often silent early on; later fatigue, edema, anemia, itching, poor appetite, and mineral and bone disease. It is staged by the GFR.
sections.typicalTreatments: Control blood pressure and diabetes, avoid nephrotoxins, manage anemia with ESAs and iron, use phosphate binders, and adjust diet. End-stage disease requires dialysis or transplant.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes, hypertension, older age, cardiovascular disease, family history, and repeated episodes of acute kidney injury.

name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
shortExplanation: A progressive, largely irreversible airflow limitation from emphysema and chronic bronchitis, most often caused by smoking, producing chronic dyspnea and cough.

sections.presentation: Chronic productive cough, progressive exertional dyspnea, wheezing, prolonged expiration, and barrel chest. Advanced disease shows pursed-lip breathing, hypoxemia, and cor pulmonale with peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Smoking cessation, long-acting bronchodilators (tiotropium, LABA), inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbations, pulmonary rehab, and long-term oxygen for chronic hypoxemia. Target controlled oxygen (SpO2 roughly 88-92 percent) to avoid CO2 retention.
sections.riskFactors: Cigarette smoking (primary), occupational dust/chemical exposure, biomass smoke, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

name: Cirrhosis
shortExplanation: Advanced scarring of the liver from chronic injury that replaces healthy tissue and impairs liver function. Leads to portal hypertension and its complications.

sections.presentation: Often silent early. Later: fatigue, jaundice, easy bruising and bleeding, ascites, leg edema, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and confusion (hepatic encephalopathy). Signs of portal hypertension include varices and an enlarged spleen.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause (alcohol cessation, antivirals for hepatitis) and manage complications: diuretics and sodium restriction for ascites, lactulose and rifaximin for encephalopathy, and variceal screening and prophylaxis. Transplant evaluation for end-stage disease.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic alcohol use, chronic hepatitis B or C, and fatty liver disease (metabolic/nonalcoholic).

name: Clostridioides difficile Infection
shortExplanation: An antibiotic-associated intestinal infection that causes profuse watery diarrhea and is spread by spores.

sections.presentation: Frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, fever, and an elevated white blood cell count, typically after recent antibiotic use.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the offending antibiotic when possible and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (metronidazole in select cases), plus fluids. Use contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene, since alcohol gel does not kill the spores. Fecal transplant is used for recurrences.
sections.riskFactors: Recent antibiotics, hospitalization, older age, and proton pump inhibitor use.

name: COPD Exacerbation
shortExplanation: Acute worsening of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease symptoms — increased shortness of breath, cough, and sputum production, often triggered by infection.

sections.presentation: Increased dyspnea, wheezing, increased sputum production or change in sputum color, use of accessory muscles, low oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bronchodilators (albuterol), corticosteroids, supplemental oxygen, antibiotics if infection is suspected, possibly BiPAP or intubation in severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking history, respiratory infection, air pollution exposure, poor medication adherence.

name: COVID-19
shortExplanation: A respiratory and multisystem illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Severity ranges from mild cold-like symptoms to severe pneumonia and respiratory failure.

sections.presentation: Fever, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, sore throat, congestion, loss of taste or smell, body aches, and GI symptoms. Severe disease brings hypoxemia, ARDS, thromboembolism, and multiorgan involvement.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supportive care and oxygen; antivirals and immunomodulators (such as corticosteroids for those needing oxygen) per current guidance; anticoagulation as indicated; prone positioning and mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemia; standard, contact, and airborne precautions per facility policy; vaccination for prevention.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular and chronic lung disease, immunocompromise, pregnancy, and being unvaccinated.

name: Crohn Disease
shortExplanation: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract, from mouth to anus, in patchy full-thickness segments. Marked by flares and remissions.

sections.presentation: Crampy abdominal pain (often right lower quadrant), chronic diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, and fever. Perianal disease (fistulas, abscesses) is common. Complications include strictures, obstruction, and fistulas. Skip lesions and transmural inflammation distinguish it from ulcerative colitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating therapy: corticosteroids for flares, immunomodulators, and biologics (anti-TNF and others). Nutritional support, smoking cessation, and surgery for complications. Monitor for malnutrition and vitamin deficiencies.
sections.riskFactors: Family history, smoking, and age (often diagnosed in adolescence or young adulthood).

name: Croup
shortExplanation: A viral infection that swells the upper airway in young children, producing a distinctive barking cough and noisy breathing.

sections.presentation: A seal-like barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor, often worse at night and preceded by cold symptoms. Retractions and stridor at rest signal more severe airway narrowing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone reduce airway swelling in most cases, and nebulized racemic epinephrine is added for moderate to severe stridor. Keep the child calm, since agitation worsens obstruction, and provide humidified air and oxygen as needed.
sections.riskFactors: Age 6 months to 3 years, fall and winter viral season, and prior episodes of croup.

name: Cushing Syndrome
shortExplanation: A disorder caused by prolonged exposure to high cortisol, most often from long-term steroid medication. Causes weight gain and characteristic body changes.

sections.presentation: Central (truncal) obesity with thin arms and legs, a rounded face, a fatty hump between the shoulders, purple stretch marks, easy bruising, thin skin, muscle weakness, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, and mood changes.
sections.typicalTreatments: For exogenous cases, gradually taper the steroid when possible. For endogenous causes, treat the source: surgery to remove a pituitary or adrenal tumor, and medications that lower cortisol. Monitor and manage hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, and infection risk.
sections.riskFactors: Long-term glucocorticoid therapy (most common), pituitary tumors (Cushing disease), adrenal tumors, and ectopic ACTH-producing tumors.

name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
shortExplanation: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, that can break loose and travel to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.

sections.presentation: Unilateral leg swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, and redness, most often in the calf; some clots are asymptomatic.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anticoagulation (heparin or LMWH transitioning to oral agents) and leg elevation. Do not massage the affected limb, which could dislodge the clot.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, recent surgery, cancer, hormone therapy, prior clots, and obesity - reflecting the Virchow triad of stasis, hypercoagulability, and vessel injury.

name: Delirium
shortExplanation: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying medical problem. It is usually reversible when the cause is treated.

sections.presentation: Acute onset with fluctuating course, inattention, disorganized thinking, altered level of consciousness. Hyperactive (agitated), hypoactive (drowsy, withdrawn), or mixed forms. Often worse at night (sundowning). Screen with tools such as CAM-ICU.
sections.typicalTreatments: Identify and treat the underlying cause (infection, hypoxia, metabolic derangement, medications, pain, urinary retention); nonpharmacologic measures first (reorientation, sleep-wake regulation, early mobility, glasses and hearing aids, minimizing lines and restraints); reserve low-dose antipsychotics for severe agitation.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, dementia, severe illness, surgery, infection, polypharmacy and sedatives, dehydration, sensory impairment, ICU stay, sleep disruption.

name: Diabetes Insipidus
shortExplanation: A disorder of water balance where the kidneys cannot concentrate urine, causing large volumes of dilute urine and intense thirst. Unrelated to blood sugar diabetes.

sections.presentation: Excessive urination (polyuria) with dilute urine, intense thirst, and frequent drinking, and risk of dehydration and hypernatremia if intake cannot keep up. Central DI results from lack of ADH; nephrogenic DI results from kidneys not responding to ADH.
sections.typicalTreatments: Central DI is treated with desmopressin (a synthetic ADH). Nephrogenic DI is managed by treating the cause, low-salt diet, and sometimes thiazide diuretics. Ensure access to water, monitor intake and output, daily weights, and sodium levels.
sections.riskFactors: Head injury, pituitary or hypothalamic surgery or tumors, certain medications (lithium for nephrogenic DI), and kidney disorders.

name: Diabetic Foot Ulcer
shortExplanation: A wound on the foot of a person with diabetes, driven by nerve damage and poor circulation, that heals slowly and can become infected.

sections.presentation: Often painless (because of neuropathy) ulcers over pressure points such as the sole or toes, frequently with surrounding callus; may show infection or poor healing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Offloading pressure from the wound, debridement, moist dressings, glucose control, treating infection, and assessing blood flow. Watch for underlying bone infection (osteomyelitis).
sections.riskFactors: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, poor glucose control, foot deformity, and prior ulcers.

name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
shortExplanation: A serious complication of diabetes where the body produces high levels of blood acids (ketones) due to insufficient insulin — a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment.

sections.presentation: Hyperglycemia, fruity-smelling breath, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations), altered mental status in severe cases.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV fluids, IV insulin infusion, potassium replacement (insulin drives potassium into cells), correction of the underlying trigger (e.g. infection, missed insulin doses).
sections.riskFactors: Missed insulin doses, infection, new-onset type 1 diabetes, physiologic stress (illness, surgery).

name: Diverticulitis
shortExplanation: Inflammation or infection of small pouches (diverticula) in the colon wall, most often in the sigmoid colon. Causes left lower quadrant pain.

sections.presentation: Left lower quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and change in bowel habits (constipation or diarrhea). Complications include abscess, perforation, obstruction, and fistula.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest and a clear liquid diet advancing as tolerated, antibiotics for complicated or higher-risk cases, and pain control. Abscesses may need drainage; perforation or recurrent disease may need surgery. A high-fiber diet is recommended to prevent recurrence.
sections.riskFactors: Age, low-fiber diet, obesity, smoking, and physical inactivity.

name: Eclampsia
shortExplanation: The onset of seizures in a woman with preeclampsia, representing a life-threatening obstetric emergency for mother and baby.

sections.presentation: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a pregnant or recently delivered woman with preeclampsia, often preceded by severe headache, visual disturbances, and hyperreflexia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway and prevent injury during the seizure, give magnesium sulfate to control and prevent further seizures, control severe hypertension, and expedite delivery once the mother is stabilized.
sections.riskFactors: Untreated or severe preeclampsia, and the same risk factors as preeclampsia.

name: Encephalitis
shortExplanation: Inflammation of the brain tissue itself, most often from a viral infection such as herpes simplex virus. It differs from meningitis by prominent brain dysfunction.

sections.presentation: Fever with altered mental status, confusion, personality or behavior changes, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and decreased level of consciousness. Headache and neck stiffness may overlap with meningitis. HSV encephalitis often affects the temporal lobes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Empiric IV acyclovir started promptly when herpes encephalitis is suspected (do not wait for confirmation); supportive ICU care, seizure control, and management of intracranial pressure; lumbar puncture with CSF PCR to identify the pathogen.
sections.riskFactors: Viral infections (HSV, arboviruses such as West Nile), immunocompromise, mosquito or tick exposure, age extremes, unvaccinated status.

name: Epilepsy (Seizure Disorder)
shortExplanation: A chronic brain disorder marked by recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal, excessive electrical activity in the brain.

sections.presentation: Varies by seizure type: generalized tonic-clonic (loss of consciousness, stiffening then rhythmic jerking, postictal confusion), focal seizures (localized motor, sensory, or behavioral changes), absence spells (brief staring). May include aura, incontinence, tongue biting.
sections.typicalTreatments: Long-term antiseizure medications (e.g. levetiracetam, phenytoin, valproate, lamotrigine); identify and avoid triggers; ketogenic diet or epilepsy surgery for refractory cases. Treat prolonged or repeated seizures as status epilepticus.
sections.riskFactors: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, brain tumor, congenital malformation, family history, alcohol or drug withdrawal, medication nonadherence, sleep deprivation.

name: Esophageal Varices
shortExplanation: Swollen, fragile veins in the lower esophagus caused by portal hypertension from cirrhosis. They can rupture and bleed massively.

sections.presentation: Often silent until they bleed. Variceal hemorrhage causes large-volume hematemesis, melena, hypotension, and shock. A history of cirrhosis or portal hypertension is typical.
sections.typicalTreatments: For acute bleeding: resuscitation, octreotide to reduce portal pressure, prophylactic antibiotics, and urgent endoscopic band ligation. Non-selective beta-blockers and banding are used to prevent bleeding. A balloon tamponade tube or TIPS procedure may be needed for uncontrolled hemorrhage.
sections.riskFactors: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension; larger varices and advanced liver disease raise bleeding risk.

name: Essential Hypertension
shortExplanation: Chronically elevated blood pressure without an identifiable secondary cause; a major modifiable risk factor for stroke, heart disease, and kidney disease.

sections.presentation: Usually asymptomatic ("silent killer") and found on routine measurement. Long-standing disease may cause headache, and end-organ damage shows as retinopathy, LVH, proteinuria, or elevated creatinine.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifestyle changes (low-sodium diet, weight loss, exercise, limiting alcohol) plus antihypertensives: thiazides (hydrochlorothiazide), ACE inhibitors/ARBs (lisinopril, losartan), and calcium channel blockers (amlodipine). Home BP monitoring and adherence are key.
sections.riskFactors: Age, family history, obesity, high sodium intake, physical inactivity, excess alcohol, and Black race.

name: Febrile Neutropenia
shortExplanation: A fever in a patient with a very low neutrophil count, treated as an oncologic emergency. Because the immune system is impaired, infection can become life-threatening within hours.

sections.presentation: A single oral temperature at or above roughly 38.3 degrees Celsius, or a sustained temperature around 38 degrees, in a neutropenic patient. Localizing signs of infection may be minimal, and the patient can deteriorate quickly to sepsis and shock.
sections.typicalTreatments: Draw blood cultures and a full workup, then start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics that cover Pseudomonas without delay, ideally within about an hour. Support hemodynamics, consider growth factors, and adjust antibiotics based on cultures and the clinical course.
sections.riskFactors: Recent chemotherapy (highest risk at the neutrophil nadir), deeper and longer neutropenia, indwelling catheters, mucositis, and older age or comorbidities.

name: Febrile Seizure
shortExplanation: A convulsion triggered by fever in a young child, usually brief and harmless, occurring most often between 6 months and 5 years of age.

sections.presentation: A generalized seizure during a febrile illness, typically lasting a few minutes, followed by drowsiness. Simple febrile seizures are brief, generalized, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex ones are prolonged, focal, or recurrent.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway and prevent injury, control the fever, and identify and treat the underlying infection. Simple febrile seizures are self-limited and generally do not require antiseizure medication. Reassure and educate caregivers.
sections.riskFactors: Age 6 months to 5 years, high or rapidly rising fever, viral infections, and a family history of febrile seizures.

name: First-Degree AV Block
shortExplanation: A conduction delay through the AV node shown as a consistently prolonged PR interval; usually benign and asymptomatic.

sections.presentation: PR interval greater than 0.20 seconds on ECG with every P wave conducting to a QRS. Patients are typically asymptomatic; found incidentally on telemetry.
sections.typicalTreatments: Usually no treatment needed. Review medications that slow AV conduction (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) and monitor for progression to higher-degree block.
sections.riskFactors: Increased vagal tone, AV-nodal blocking drugs, aging conduction system, ischemia, and electrolyte disturbances.

name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
shortExplanation: Chronic backflow of stomach acid into the esophagus, causing heartburn and regurgitation. Long-standing reflux can injure the esophageal lining.

sections.presentation: Heartburn (burning behind the breastbone), acid regurgitation, worse when lying flat or after meals. May cause chronic cough, hoarseness, sore throat, or a sensation of a lump in the throat. Chest pain that can mimic cardiac pain.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifestyle changes (weight loss, elevating the head of the bed, avoiding late meals and trigger foods), acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers, and antacids for breakthrough symptoms. Surgery (fundoplication) for refractory cases.
sections.riskFactors: Obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol, large or fatty meals, and delayed gastric emptying.

name: Gastrointestinal Bleed
shortExplanation: Bleeding anywhere along the digestive tract, which can range from slow and hidden to rapid and life-threatening.

sections.presentation: Upper GI bleeds cause vomiting of blood or coffee-ground material and black tarry stools (melena); lower GI bleeds cause bright red blood per rectum. Large bleeds cause fatigue, low blood pressure, and a fast heart rate.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV access and fluids, blood transfusion as needed, proton pump inhibitors, endoscopy to locate and treat the source, and holding anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs.
sections.riskFactors: NSAID or aspirin use, anticoagulation, peptic ulcer disease, liver disease with varices, and H. pylori infection.

name: Guillain-Barre Syndrome
shortExplanation: An autoimmune disorder in which the body attacks peripheral nerves, causing rapidly progressive, usually ascending muscle weakness. It often follows a recent infection.

sections.presentation: Symmetric ascending weakness starting in the legs, diminished or absent reflexes, paresthesias, and possible progression to respiratory muscle and cranial nerve involvement. Autonomic instability (blood pressure and heart rate swings) can occur.
sections.typicalTreatments: IVIG or plasmapheresis; close monitoring of respiratory function with serial vital capacity and negative inspiratory force; intubation and mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure develops; DVT prophylaxis and supportive care; rehabilitation during recovery.
sections.riskFactors: Recent respiratory or GI infection (notably Campylobacter jejuni), recent viral illness, occasionally recent surgery or vaccination.

name: HELLP Syndrome
shortExplanation: A severe variant of preeclampsia defined by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets that can rapidly threaten the mother's life.

sections.presentation: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, malaise, and headache, often with hypertension. Labs show breakdown of red cells, elevated liver enzymes, and a falling platelet count.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, blood pressure control, correction of coagulation problems, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm, and prompt delivery.
sections.riskFactors: Preeclampsia, prior HELLP, and multiparity; it can occur even when blood pressure elevation is only mild.

name: Hemoptysis
shortExplanation: Coughing up blood or blood-streaked sputum from the lower respiratory tract; massive hemoptysis is a life-threatening airway emergency.

sections.presentation: Blood-tinged or frankly bloody sputum, often frothy and bright red. Massive hemoptysis presents with large-volume bleeding, respiratory distress, and risk of asphyxiation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway, position bleeding side down, provide oxygen, and correct coagulopathy. Bronchoscopy, CT angiography, and bronchial artery embolization localize and control bleeding; treat the underlying cause.
sections.riskFactors: Bronchitis, bronchiectasis, tuberculosis and other infections, lung cancer, pulmonary embolism, anticoagulation, and vasculitis.

name: Hemorrhagic Stroke
shortExplanation: Bleeding into or around the brain from a ruptured vessel, causing sudden neurologic deficits and dangerous pressure on brain tissue.

sections.presentation: Sudden severe headache (often described as the worst ever), vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, focal weakness or speech changes, seizures, and signs of rising intracranial pressure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent CT to confirm and locate bleeding, tight blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation, and management of intracranial pressure (hyperosmolar therapy, head-of-bed elevation). Neurosurgical intervention for select cases.
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension, anticoagulant use, aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation, older age, and heavy alcohol use.

name: Hepatic Encephalopathy
shortExplanation: Brain dysfunction from a failing liver's inability to clear toxins such as ammonia. Causes confusion ranging from subtle to coma.

sections.presentation: Confusion, personality changes, sleep reversal, and slurred speech progressing to lethargy and coma. Asterixis (a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands) is characteristic. Often elevated blood ammonia, though levels correlate poorly with severity.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lactulose to trap and eliminate ammonia through the stool (titrated to 2-3 soft stools daily), rifaximin to reduce ammonia-producing gut bacteria, and identifying precipitants (GI bleeding, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbances, dehydration). Protect the airway if obtunded.
sections.riskFactors: Cirrhosis or acute liver failure, GI bleeding, infection, constipation, dehydration, and sedating medications.

name: HIV / AIDS
shortExplanation: Human immunodeficiency virus infection progressively weakens the immune system by attacking CD4 T-cells; advanced infection is called AIDS. Treatment allows many to live long, healthy lives.

sections.presentation: Acute infection may cause a flu-like or mononucleosis-like illness. Without treatment, progressive immune decline leads to opportunistic infections and cancers (AIDS-defining illnesses) as the CD4 count falls. Many are asymptomatic for years.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) to suppress the virus and preserve immune function; prophylaxis against opportunistic infections at low CD4 counts; treat coinfections; standard precautions; pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis for prevention. Monitor viral load and CD4 count.
sections.riskFactors: Unprotected sex, sharing injection equipment, exposure to infected blood or body fluids, perinatal transmission, and other sexually transmitted infections.

name: Hypercalcemia
shortExplanation: A higher-than-normal blood calcium level that slows nerve and muscle activity. Most often caused by overactive parathyroid glands or cancer.

sections.presentation: Often summarized as 'stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric moans': kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea, and confusion or depression. Also increased thirst and urination, muscle weakness, and a shortened QT interval. Severe cases cause lethargy and coma.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV isotonic fluids to restore volume and promote calcium excretion, and bisphosphonates or calcitonin to lower calcium, especially in malignancy. Treat the underlying cause; avoid thiazide diuretics. Monitor cardiac rhythm, fluid status, and calcium trend.
sections.riskFactors: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, prolonged immobilization, excessive vitamin D or calcium intake, and certain medications (thiazides, lithium).

name: Hyperkalemia
shortExplanation: A high blood potassium level that can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes and is common in kidney failure.

sections.presentation: Often no symptoms; may cause muscle weakness. Cardiac effects include peaked T waves, a widening QRS, and risk of fatal arrhythmias.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV calcium to stabilize the heart; insulin with glucose and inhaled albuterol to shift potassium into cells; and removal of potassium with diuretics, binders (SPS or patiromer), or dialysis.
sections.riskFactors: Kidney disease, potassium-sparing drugs and ACE inhibitors, tissue breakdown, acidosis, and large blood transfusions.

name: Hyperlipidemia
shortExplanation: Elevated blood cholesterol and/or triglycerides that promote atherosclerosis, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.

sections.presentation: Usually asymptomatic and detected on a lipid panel. Severe cases may show xanthomas, xanthelasma, or corneal arcus; very high triglycerides can trigger pancreatitis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Diet (reduce saturated fat), exercise, weight loss, and smoking cessation, plus statins (atorvastatin) as first-line drug therapy; ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, or fibrates when needed. Monitor lipid panel and liver enzymes.
sections.riskFactors: Diet high in saturated/trans fats, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and genetics (familial hypercholesterolemia).

name: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
shortExplanation: A life-threatening complication of type 2 diabetes with extremely high blood sugar and severe dehydration, but little or no ketoacidosis.

sections.presentation: Very high blood glucose (often above 600 mg/dL), profound dehydration, increased thirst and urination, and altered mental status ranging from confusion to coma. High serum osmolality. Unlike DKA, minimal ketones and little or no acidosis. Often develops over days.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is the priority, then insulin infusion to lower glucose gradually, and careful correction of electrolytes (especially potassium). Identify and treat the precipitant (often infection). Monitor glucose, electrolytes, and neurologic status closely.
sections.riskFactors: Type 2 diabetes (often previously undiagnosed), older age, infection or acute illness, poor access to fluids, and missed medications.

name: Hypertensive Crisis
shortExplanation: Severely elevated blood pressure. When it starts damaging organs (brain, heart, kidneys) it's an emergency needing carefully controlled lowering.

sections.presentation: Very high BP (often >180/120); emergency if with target-organ signs: headache, vision changes, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or neuro deficits.
sections.typicalTreatments: Hypertensive emergency: IV agents (e.g. nicardipine, labetalol) with gradual, controlled BP reduction to avoid hypoperfusion; hypertensive urgency: oral agents and close follow-up.
sections.riskFactors: Poorly controlled or untreated hypertension, medication non-adherence, kidney disease, stimulant use.

name: Hyperthyroidism
shortExplanation: An overactive thyroid producing too much thyroid hormone, speeding up metabolism. Graves disease is the most common cause.

sections.presentation: Weight loss despite good appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, and frequent stools. Graves disease can cause a goiter and bulging eyes (exophthalmos). Labs show a low TSH with elevated thyroid hormones.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antithyroid medications (methimazole, or propylthiouracil in specific situations), beta-blockers to control symptoms such as tachycardia and tremor, radioactive iodine ablation, or thyroidectomy. Monitor heart rate and rhythm.
sections.riskFactors: Graves disease (autoimmune), toxic nodular goiter, thyroiditis, excess iodine, and female sex.

name: Hypocalcemia
shortExplanation: A lower-than-normal blood calcium level that increases nerve and muscle excitability, causing cramps, tingling, and, when severe, tetany or seizures.

sections.presentation: Numbness and tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, muscle cramps, and hyperactive reflexes. Classic signs are Chvostek sign (facial twitch when tapping the cheek) and Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with a blood pressure cuff). Severe cases cause tetany, laryngospasm, prolonged QT interval, and seizures.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral or IV calcium replacement depending on severity and symptoms; IV calcium (such as calcium gluconate) for severe or symptomatic cases. Replace vitamin D and correct low magnesium, which can cause refractory hypocalcemia. Use continuous cardiac monitoring during IV calcium.
sections.riskFactors: Hypoparathyroidism (including after thyroid or parathyroid surgery), vitamin D deficiency, low magnesium, kidney disease, and pancreatitis.

name: Hypoglycemia
shortExplanation: A low blood glucose level that can quickly cause confusion and, if untreated, loss of consciousness or seizures.

sections.presentation: Shakiness, sweating, palpitations, and hunger, progressing to confusion and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness or seizures. It is typically defined as glucose below about 70 mg/dL.
sections.typicalTreatments: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate (juice or glucose tablets) if the patient is awake and able to swallow; use IV dextrose or IM glucagon if they cannot. Recheck glucose and re-treat as needed (the rule of 15).
sections.riskFactors: Insulin or sulfonylureas, missed meals, kidney disease, alcohol, and tighter glucose targets.

name: Hypomagnesemia
shortExplanation: A lower-than-normal blood magnesium level that increases neuromuscular and cardiac excitability. Frequently occurs alongside low potassium and low calcium.

sections.presentation: Muscle cramps, twitching, tremor, weakness, and hyperactive reflexes; severe cases cause seizures and dangerous heart arrhythmias (including torsades de pointes) and a prolonged QT interval. Often accompanies and worsens hypokalemia and hypocalcemia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium replacement, oral for mild deficiency and IV magnesium sulfate for severe or symptomatic cases. Because low magnesium makes potassium and calcium hard to correct, replace magnesium to fix those as well. Use cardiac monitoring with IV replacement and monitor reflexes.
sections.riskFactors: Alcohol use disorder, poor intake or malnutrition, GI losses (diarrhea, malabsorption), diuretics and proton pump inhibitors, and refeeding syndrome.

name: Hyponatremia
shortExplanation: A low blood sodium level, the most common electrolyte disorder, which in severe cases causes brain swelling.

sections.presentation: Headache, nausea, confusion, and lethargy; severe or rapid drops can cause seizures and cerebral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Depends on the cause and fluid status - fluid restriction, treating the underlying cause, or careful hypertonic saline for severe symptoms. Correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
sections.riskFactors: SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis, diuretics, excess water intake, and older age.

name: Hypothyroidism
shortExplanation: An underactive thyroid that produces too little thyroid hormone, slowing the body's metabolism. Most often caused by autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis.

sections.presentation: Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, depression, and slowed thinking. Labs show a high TSH with a low free T4 in primary disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Lifelong thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, titrated by monitoring TSH. Take on an empty stomach and separate from interfering foods and medications. Symptoms improve gradually over weeks.
sections.riskFactors: Autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, prior thyroid surgery or radioiodine, certain medications (amiodarone, lithium), iodine deficiency, and female sex.

name: Hypovolemic Shock
shortExplanation: Shock caused by a large loss of blood or fluid, so there is not enough volume to perfuse the organs.

sections.presentation: Fast, weak pulse, low blood pressure, cool and clammy skin, rapid breathing, thirst, low urine output, and confusion. With hemorrhage there may be obvious or hidden bleeding.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the source of loss (control bleeding), rapid IV fluid or blood product resuscitation, and treat the underlying cause. Massive transfusion protocol for severe hemorrhage. Vasopressors are a temporizing measure, not a substitute for volume.
sections.riskFactors: Trauma, gastrointestinal or surgical bleeding, ruptured aneurysm, severe vomiting or diarrhea, burns, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

name: Increased Intracranial Pressure
shortExplanation: Dangerously high pressure inside the skull that reduces blood flow to the brain and can cause brain tissue to shift or herniate.

sections.presentation: Headache, vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, and pupil changes. Late signs include the Cushing triad (rising blood pressure, slow heart rate, irregular breathing) and posturing, which signal impending herniation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Elevate the head of the bed and keep the neck midline, ensure oxygenation and normal carbon dioxide, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), sedation and analgesia, and CSF drainage via an external ventricular drain. Neurosurgery for select causes.
sections.riskFactors: Traumatic brain injury, hemorrhagic stroke, large ischemic stroke, brain tumor, hydrocephalus, and CNS infection.

name: Infective Endocarditis
shortExplanation: An infection of the heart's inner lining or valves, usually bacterial — dangerous because clumps of infection can break off and travel through the body.

sections.presentation: Fever, new or changed heart murmur, fatigue; classic embolic/immune signs (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages), positive blood cultures, vegetations on echo.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged IV antibiotics guided by cultures, blood cultures before antibiotics, surgery for valve destruction or persistent infection, monitor for embolic complications.
sections.riskFactors: Prosthetic heart valve, IV drug use, structural heart disease, indwelling lines, prior endocarditis.

name: Influenza
shortExplanation: A contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It can cause mild to severe disease and dangerous complications, especially in high-risk groups.

sections.presentation: Abrupt fever, chills, myalgias, headache, fatigue, dry cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion. Complications include pneumonia (viral or secondary bacterial), worsening of chronic conditions, and respiratory failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supportive care and antipyretics; antiviral medications (such as oseltamivir) are most effective when started early, especially for high-risk or hospitalized patients; droplet precautions; annual vaccination for prevention.
sections.riskFactors: Age extremes, pregnancy, chronic lung, heart, kidney, or metabolic disease, immunocompromise, obesity, and residence in long-term care.

name: Kawasaki Disease
shortExplanation: An acute inflammation of blood vessels in young children that, if untreated, can damage the coronary arteries of the heart.

sections.presentation: Fever lasting five or more days plus features such as bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge, cracked red lips and strawberry tongue, rash, swelling and redness of the hands and feet with later peeling, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Children are typically very irritable.
sections.typicalTreatments: Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) and aspirin to reduce inflammation and lower the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Echocardiography is used to monitor the coronary arteries. Prompt treatment within the first days of illness improves outcomes.
sections.riskFactors: Age under 5 years, male sex, and Asian ancestry, though it occurs in all populations.

name: Malignant Hyperthermia
shortExplanation: A rare, inherited, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. It is an anesthesia emergency treated with dantrolene.

sections.presentation: Early signs are an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, and masseter or generalized muscle rigidity. Later signs include a rapidly rising temperature, mixed acidosis, hyperkalemia, dark cola-colored urine from rhabdomyolysis, and unstable vital signs.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediately stop the triggering agent and call for the MH cart, give IV dantrolene, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, and start active cooling. Treat hyperkalemia and acidosis, support urine output, and monitor for recurrence in the ICU.
sections.riskFactors: Inherited RYR1 or related gene mutation (autosomal dominant), personal or family history of an MH event or of certain muscle disorders, and exposure to volatile anesthetics (such as sevoflurane) or succinylcholine.

name: MRSA Infection
shortExplanation: An infection caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium resistant to many common antibiotics. It ranges from skin infections to life-threatening bloodstream or lung infections.

sections.presentation: Skin and soft-tissue infections (red, swollen, painful areas, abscesses, or 'spider bite'-like lesions) are common; invasive disease can cause bacteremia, pneumonia, endocarditis, bone infection, and sepsis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Drainage of abscesses; antibiotics active against MRSA such as vancomycin or others based on culture and sensitivity; source control; contact precautions to limit spread. De-escalate therapy per culture results.
sections.riskFactors: Recent hospitalization or surgery, indwelling devices and catheters, hemodialysis, crowded settings, injection drug use, prior antibiotic exposure, and skin breakdown.

name: Mucositis
shortExplanation: Painful inflammation and ulceration of the mucous membranes lining the mouth and GI tract, caused by chemotherapy or radiation. Oral mucositis can make eating, drinking, and swallowing very difficult.

sections.presentation: Redness, soreness, swelling, and ulcers of the mouth and throat, pain with eating or swallowing, and sometimes bleeding. It can extend along the GI tract, causing diarrhea, and open sores create a route for infection.
sections.typicalTreatments: Frequent gentle oral care with a soft brush and bland rinses, topical and systemic analgesia (including opioids for severe pain), treating superimposed infections such as candidiasis, and supporting nutrition and hydration. Cryotherapy (ice chips) during certain infusions can help prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: Chemotherapy (especially agents like fluorouracil and methotrexate), head and neck radiation, high-dose therapy and transplant conditioning, neutropenia, and poor baseline oral hygiene.

name: Multiple Sclerosis
shortExplanation: A chronic autoimmune disease that damages the myelin covering nerves in the brain and spinal cord, disrupting nerve signaling. It commonly follows a relapsing-remitting course.

sections.presentation: Variable and often relapsing: vision changes (optic neuritis), numbness or tingling, weakness, spasticity, fatigue, gait and balance problems, bladder dysfunction, and cognitive changes. Symptoms may worsen with heat.
sections.typicalTreatments: Disease-modifying therapies to reduce relapses; corticosteroids for acute relapses; symptom management for spasticity, fatigue, pain, and bladder issues; physical and occupational rehabilitation.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex, ages roughly 20 to 40 at onset, higher latitudes, low vitamin D, family history, smoking, certain viral exposures.

name: Myasthenia Gravis
shortExplanation: An autoimmune disease where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity.

sections.presentation: Fatigable weakness worsening through the day and with use: ptosis, diplopia, difficulty chewing or swallowing, slurred speech, and proximal limb weakness. Severe cases threaten respiratory muscles.
sections.typicalTreatments: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine); immunosuppression (corticosteroids, other agents); thymectomy in selected patients; IVIG or plasmapheresis for crisis. Avoid medications that worsen weakness.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex in younger adults, male sex in older adults, thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, other autoimmune diseases.

name: Myasthenic Crisis
shortExplanation: A life-threatening worsening of myasthenia gravis in which respiratory muscle weakness leads to respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support.

sections.presentation: Rapidly worsening generalized and respiratory weakness, dyspnea, weak cough, difficulty clearing secretions, dysphagia, and declining vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, progressing to respiratory failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Airway protection and mechanical ventilation as needed; IVIG or plasmapheresis; identify and treat triggers (infection, certain medications, surgery, tapering of immunotherapy); ICU monitoring of respiratory parameters. Distinguish from cholinergic crisis.
sections.riskFactors: Infection, aspiration, surgery, pregnancy, physiologic stress, undertreatment or abrupt medication changes, drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission.

name: Myxedema Coma
shortExplanation: A rare, life-threatening extreme of severe hypothyroidism, marked by altered mental status, hypothermia, and slowed body functions. A medical emergency.

sections.presentation: Decreased mental status or coma, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, and hyponatremia and hypoglycemia. Often precipitated by infection, cold exposure, surgery, or sedating drugs in a person with underlying hypothyroidism.
sections.typicalTreatments: ICU care with IV thyroid hormone replacement, IV corticosteroids (given until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), gentle rewarming, ventilatory and hemodynamic support, and treating the trigger. Correct hyponatremia and hypoglycemia carefully.
sections.riskFactors: Undertreated hypothyroidism plus a precipitant such as infection, cold, surgery, or sedatives; more common in older women in winter.

name: Necrotizing Enterocolitis
shortExplanation: A serious intestinal disease of mostly premature infants in which the bowel becomes inflamed and can die, sometimes leading to perforation.

sections.presentation: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and tenderness, bloody stools, bilious gastric residuals, and systemic signs such as lethargy, apnea, and temperature instability. Abdominal x-ray may show gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis).
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop feeds and rest the gut (NPO), decompress the stomach with a tube, give IV fluids, nutrition, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and monitor closely. Surgery is needed if the bowel perforates or the infant deteriorates.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity and low birth weight, formula feeding, rapid advancement of feeds, and conditions reducing intestinal blood flow.

name: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia
shortExplanation: A high level of bilirubin in a newborn that causes jaundice, and if severe and untreated can injure the brain.

sections.presentation: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes, typically starting on the face and progressing downward, along with sleepiness or poor feeding when severe. Bilirubin levels are trended against age in hours.
sections.typicalTreatments: Phototherapy to break down bilirubin, ensuring adequate feeding and hydration to promote excretion, and exchange transfusion for dangerously high levels. Very high untreated bilirubin can cause kernicterus, a permanent brain injury.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity, blood type incompatibility between mother and baby, bruising or cephalohematoma, poor feeding, and a sibling who required phototherapy.

name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
shortExplanation: A breathing disorder of premature newborns caused by a lack of surfactant, which keeps the tiny air sacs in the lungs from staying open.

sections.presentation: Within hours of birth a preterm infant develops tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions, and cyanosis, with worsening oxygenation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Exogenous surfactant given through the breathing tube, respiratory support with CPAP or mechanical ventilation, and supplemental oxygen. Antenatal corticosteroids given to the mother before preterm birth help prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity (the more premature, the higher the risk), maternal diabetes, cesarean delivery without labor, and lack of antenatal steroids.

name: Neonatal Sepsis
shortExplanation: A bloodstream infection in a newborn that can progress rapidly and requires prompt recognition and antibiotics.

sections.presentation: Often subtle and nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or low temperature), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, apnea, respiratory distress, and poor perfusion. Early-onset appears within the first days of life and late-onset after.
