sections.typicalTreatments: Obtain blood cultures and other cultures, then start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (commonly ampicillin plus gentamicin) without delay, and provide supportive care for breathing and circulation. Narrow therapy once culture results return.
sections.riskFactors: Maternal group B strep colonization, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, prematurity, and invasive lines or devices.

name: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
shortExplanation: A rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) medications marked by high fever and severe muscle rigidity.

sections.presentation: High fever, generalized lead-pipe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability (fluctuating blood pressure, tachycardia, sweating). Laboratory tests often show a markedly elevated creatine kinase. It usually develops over days.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediately stop the offending antipsychotic, provide aggressive supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, and use medications such as dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases. Monitor for complications like kidney injury from muscle breakdown.
sections.riskFactors: Starting or increasing antipsychotics, high-potency agents, rapid dose escalation, dehydration, and abruptly stopping dopaminergic medications.

name: Neutropenia
shortExplanation: An abnormally low number of neutrophils, the white blood cells that fight bacterial infection. It is a common effect of chemotherapy and greatly raises infection risk.

sections.presentation: Often asymptomatic until infection develops. Because there are few neutrophils, the usual signs of infection may be blunted, so fever may be the only clue. Severity is graded by the absolute neutrophil count (ANC), with an ANC below 500 considered severe.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat and prevent infection with meticulous hand hygiene and neutropenic precautions, prompt evaluation of any fever, growth factor support such as filgrastim when indicated, and delaying or dose-reducing chemotherapy when counts are too low.
sections.riskFactors: Cytotoxic chemotherapy (the most common cause), radiation, bone marrow cancers and transplant, certain drugs, and severe infection. Risk of serious infection rises as the count falls and the neutropenic period lengthens.

name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
shortExplanation: Repeated collapse of the upper airway during sleep causing pauses in breathing, oxygen desaturation, and fragmented sleep.

sections.presentation: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping/choking at night, daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, and difficulty concentrating. Often accompanied by hypertension and obesity.
sections.typicalTreatments: CPAP is first-line; weight loss, positional therapy, oral appliances, and avoiding alcohol/sedatives at night. Diagnosis confirmed by polysomnography (sleep study).
sections.riskFactors: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, older age, enlarged tonsils, and alcohol or sedative use.

name: Opioid Withdrawal
shortExplanation: The uncomfortable but usually not life-threatening symptoms that occur when someone dependent on opioids stops or cuts back.

sections.presentation: Anxiety and drug craving, muscle aches, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, runny nose and tearing, yawning, sweating, dilated pupils, goosebumps, and restlessness. Symptoms are very distressing but rarely dangerous in otherwise healthy adults.
sections.typicalTreatments: Medications such as buprenorphine or methadone ease withdrawal and support recovery, and clonidine helps with autonomic symptoms. Symptomatic care addresses nausea, diarrhea, and muscle aches. Severity is often tracked with the COWS scale.
sections.riskFactors: Physical dependence from chronic opioid use, abrupt cessation, and administration of an opioid antagonist such as naloxone or naltrexone.

name: Osteomyelitis
shortExplanation: An infection of bone, usually bacterial, that can arise from the bloodstream, adjacent tissue infection, or a wound. It often requires prolonged antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

sections.presentation: Localized bone pain, warmth, swelling, and tenderness; fever and malaise; a draining sinus tract or non-healing wound in chronic cases (common in diabetic foot ulcers). Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) support the diagnosis; imaging and bone culture confirm it.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged, often IV, antibiotics guided by culture and sensitivity (frequently weeks); surgical debridement or removal of infected or dead bone and hardware when needed; source control and glucose optimization in diabetics.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes and peripheral vascular disease, open fractures or orthopedic hardware, pressure injuries, IV drug use, recent surgery, and immunocompromise.

name: Otitis Media
shortExplanation: A middle ear infection that is one of the most common illnesses of early childhood, causing ear pain and fever.

sections.presentation: Ear pain, tugging at the ear in nonverbal children, fever, irritability, trouble sleeping, and sometimes drainage if the eardrum ruptures. The eardrum appears red, bulging, and poorly mobile on exam.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pain and fever control with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and antibiotics such as amoxicillin when treatment is indicated. Some cases are observed without antibiotics. Recurrent infections may lead to ear tube placement.
sections.riskFactors: Young age, daycare attendance, bottle feeding while lying down, pacifier use, secondhand smoke, and recent upper respiratory infection.

name: Parkinson Disease
shortExplanation: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder from loss of dopamine-producing neurons, causing tremor, stiffness, and slowed movement.

sections.presentation: Resting tremor (often 'pill-rolling'), bradykinesia, rigidity (cogwheeling), postural instability, shuffling festinating gait, masked facial expression, soft speech, micrographia, and later cognitive and autonomic changes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Dopaminergic therapy, especially levodopa-carbidopa; dopamine agonists and other adjuncts; deep brain stimulation for select advanced cases; physical, occupational, and speech therapy; fall prevention and careful timing of medication doses.
sections.riskFactors: Advancing age, male sex, family history, certain pesticide or toxin exposures.

name: Pediatric Asthma Exacerbation
shortExplanation: An acute flare of asthma in a child, with narrowing of the airways causing wheezing, cough, and increased work of breathing.

sections.presentation: Wheezing, cough, chest tightness, prolonged expiration, retractions, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles. Severe attacks may show a silent chest, inability to speak in full sentences, and falling oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Inhaled short-acting bronchodilators (albuterol), often with ipratropium in the acute setting, systemic corticosteroids, and supplemental oxygen. Severe cases may need continuous nebulization or magnesium. Reassess respiratory effort and oxygenation frequently.
sections.riskFactors: Known asthma, viral respiratory infections, allergen or smoke exposure, exercise, cold air, and poor adherence to controller medications.

name: Pediatric Dehydration
shortExplanation: A loss of body fluids in children, often from vomiting and diarrhea, that can progress quickly and become dangerous in infants.

sections.presentation: Dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output and fewer wet diapers, absent tears, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, and lethargy. In infants a sunken fontanelle is a sign, and severe cases show tachycardia and low blood pressure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral rehydration therapy is preferred for mild to moderate dehydration, given in small frequent amounts. IV fluids are used for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, or shock. Treat the underlying cause and monitor weight, urine output, and electrolytes.
sections.riskFactors: Gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea, young age, fever, poor oral intake, and limited access to fluids.

name: Peptic Ulcer Disease
shortExplanation: Open sores in the lining of the stomach or first part of the small intestine, most often from H. pylori infection or NSAID use. Can bleed or perforate.

sections.presentation: Burning or gnawing upper abdominal pain, often related to meals (gastric ulcers worse with food, duodenal ulcers relieved by food and worse at night). Bloating, nausea. Bleeding presents as melena, hematemesis, or coffee-ground emesis; perforation causes sudden severe pain and a rigid abdomen.
sections.typicalTreatments: Proton pump inhibitors to suppress acid and promote healing, H. pylori eradication with combination antibiotics plus a PPI, and stopping NSAIDs. Endoscopy to diagnose and treat bleeding; surgery for perforation.
sections.riskFactors: H. pylori infection, chronic NSAID or aspirin use, smoking, alcohol, and physiologic stress (critical illness).

name: Pericarditis
shortExplanation: Inflammation of the sac around the heart, causing sharp chest pain that often eases when sitting forward. Usually treatable, but can lead to fluid buildup.

sections.presentation: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG.
sections.typicalTreatments: NSAIDs and colchicine, treat the underlying cause, monitor for progression to a pericardial effusion or tamponade.
sections.riskFactors: Recent viral infection, recent MI (Dressler syndrome), cardiac surgery, autoimmune disease, uremia.

name: Perioperative Hypothermia
shortExplanation: An unintended drop in core body temperature below about 36 degrees Celsius around the time of surgery. Anesthesia impairs the body's ability to hold heat in a cold operating room.

sections.presentation: Low core temperature, shivering on emergence, cold extremities, and patient-reported chilling. It contributes to discomfort and delayed recovery.
sections.typicalTreatments: Active warming with forced-air warming blankets, warmed IV fluids and irrigation, raising the ambient temperature, and covering exposed skin. Prewarming before induction helps prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: General or neuraxial anesthesia, cold operating rooms, long procedures, large exposed surgical fields, extremes of age, low body weight, and infusion of cool fluids. Consequences include increased surgical site infection, coagulopathy and bleeding, cardiac events, and prolonged drug effects.

name: Peripheral Arterial Disease
shortExplanation: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries to the limbs (usually legs) that reduces blood flow, causing pain with walking and, if severe, tissue loss.

sections.presentation: Intermittent claudication (calf pain with walking relieved by rest), cool pale extremities, diminished or absent distal pulses, hair loss, shiny skin, and slow-healing wounds. Critical limb ischemia causes rest pain and ulcers/gangrene.
sections.typicalTreatments: Smoking cessation, supervised exercise, statins, antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel), and BP/diabetes control. Revascularization (angioplasty, stenting, or bypass) for severe disease. Meticulous foot care.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, older age, and known coronary or cerebrovascular disease.

name: Placental Abruption
shortExplanation: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall before delivery, which can cut off the baby's oxygen supply and cause dangerous maternal bleeding.

sections.presentation: Sudden painful vaginal bleeding, a firm, tender, or rigid uterus, frequent contractions, and often a nonreassuring or absent fetal heart rate. Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so blood loss can be underestimated.
sections.typicalTreatments: Continuous fetal and maternal monitoring, IV access and fluid or blood resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often cesarean) when the mother or fetus is unstable. Watch for disseminated intravascular coagulation.
sections.riskFactors: Maternal hypertension or preeclampsia, abdominal trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, advanced maternal age, and multiple gestation.

name: Pleural Effusion
shortExplanation: An abnormal collection of fluid in the pleural space that compresses the lung and causes dyspnea; classified as transudative or exudative by cause.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the fluid, decreased tactile fremitus, and sometimes pleuritic chest pain or cough.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause; thoracentesis for diagnosis and symptom relief; chest tube for large or infected (empyema) effusions; diuresis for heart-failure-related transudates.
sections.riskFactors: Heart failure, pneumonia, malignancy, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, pulmonary embolism, and recent cardiothoracic surgery.

name: Pneumonia
shortExplanation: An infection of the lung tissue that fills air sacs with fluid or pus, causing cough, fever, and difficulty breathing.

sections.presentation: Cough (often productive), fever, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, crackles on auscultation, and low oxygen saturation. Older adults may present with new confusion or falls rather than classic symptoms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics guided by whether it is community- or hospital-acquired, supplemental oxygen, fluids, antipyretics, and pulmonary hygiene such as incentive spirometry and early mobility.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, smoking, COPD, immobility, aspiration risk, recent hospitalization, and immunosuppression.

name: Pneumothorax
shortExplanation: Air trapped in the pleural space that collapses part of the lung, causing sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.

sections.presentation: Sudden, sharp, one-sided pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, decreased or absent breath sounds and hyperresonance over the affected side, and tachypnea.
sections.typicalTreatments: Small stable pneumothoraces may be observed with oxygen; larger or symptomatic ones need needle aspiration or chest tube drainage. Supplemental oxygen speeds reabsorption of pleural air.
sections.riskFactors: Tall thin young males (primary spontaneous), COPD or other lung disease (secondary), chest trauma, and invasive procedures such as central line placement or thoracentesis.

name: Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
shortExplanation: Nausea and vomiting occurring in the first day or so after anesthesia and surgery. It is one of the most common and distressing complications for surgical patients.

sections.presentation: Nausea, retching, and vomiting in the recovery unit or on the ward after surgery, which can delay discharge and, rarely, cause aspiration or wound strain.
sections.typicalTreatments: Multimodal prophylaxis and treatment with antiemetics from different classes (for example a serotonin antagonist plus dexamethasone), reducing opioids with multimodal analgesia, adequate hydration, and using regional or total IV anesthesia in high-risk patients.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex, nonsmoking status, history of PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioid use are the main risk factors (Apfel score); volatile anesthetics, nitrous oxide, and certain surgery types also increase risk.

name: Postpartum Hemorrhage
shortExplanation: Excessive bleeding after childbirth, a leading cause of maternal death that requires rapid recognition and treatment.

sections.presentation: Heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery, a soft (boggy) or poorly contracted uterus, passage of large clots, and signs of blood loss such as tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor.
sections.typicalTreatments: The cause is often summarized as the four Ts: Tone (uterine atony, the most common), Trauma (lacerations), Tissue (retained placenta), and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Management includes firm fundal massage, uterotonic medications (oxytocin, methylergonovine, misoprostol, carboprost), IV fluids and blood products, and procedures such as uterine tamponade or surgery if bleeding continues.
sections.riskFactors: Uterine atony, prolonged or induced labor, overdistended uterus (large baby, twins, polyhydramnios), retained placenta, operative delivery, and clotting disorders.

name: Preeclampsia
shortExplanation: A pregnancy complication of new high blood pressure with signs of organ stress (such as protein in the urine) after 20 weeks of gestation.

sections.presentation: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or other end-organ signs. Warning features include severe headache, visual changes (blurring, flashing lights), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, rapid swelling, and shortness of breath.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease, antihypertensives such as labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine for dangerous blood pressures, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm, and ultimately delivery, which is the definitive treatment.
sections.riskFactors: First pregnancy, prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, obesity, multiple gestation, and extremes of maternal age.

name: Pressure Injury
shortExplanation: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue from sustained pressure over a bony prominence, staged by depth.

sections.presentation: Staged as: Stage 1 (intact skin with non-blanchable redness), Stage 2 (partial-thickness loss or blister), Stage 3 (full-thickness loss into fat), and Stage 4 (exposed muscle, tendon, or bone). Unstageable wounds are covered by slough or eschar; deep tissue injury shows persistent maroon or purple discoloration.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pressure redistribution with repositioning and support surfaces, offloading, moisture and nutrition management, stage-appropriate dressings, and debridement of nonviable tissue.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, poor nutrition, moisture and incontinence, friction and shear, reduced sensation, and poor perfusion; risk is screened with tools such as the Braden scale.

name: Pulmonary Embolism
shortExplanation: A blockage in a lung artery, usually caused by a blood clot that traveled from the legs (DVT) — a potentially life-threatening emergency.

sections.presentation: Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain (often pleuritic), tachycardia, low oxygen saturation, sometimes hemoptysis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anticoagulation (heparin, then often transitioned to an oral anticoagulant), thrombolytics in severe/massive PE, supportive oxygen therapy.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, recent surgery, DVT history, cancer, pregnancy, clotting disorders.

name: Pulmonary Hypertension
shortExplanation: Elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries that strains the right heart and can progress to right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

sections.presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope, a loud pulmonic heart sound, and signs of right heart failure such as jugular venous distension, ascites, and peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause (left heart disease, lung disease, chronic PE); pulmonary vasodilators for select types; diuretics for volume overload; and long-term oxygen for hypoxemia.
sections.riskFactors: Left heart failure, COPD and chronic lung disease, chronic thromboembolic disease, obstructive sleep apnea, connective tissue disease, and certain congenital heart defects.

name: Respiratory Acidosis
shortExplanation: A drop in blood pH from inadequate ventilation causing CO2 retention (hypercapnia); the lungs fail to blow off enough carbon dioxide.

sections.presentation: Low pH with high PaCO2 on ABG. Signs include headache, drowsiness, confusion, flushed skin, and (in acute cases) somnolence progressing to CO2 narcosis. Chronic cases show renal compensation with elevated bicarbonate.
sections.typicalTreatments: Improve ventilation: bronchodilators, reversal of sedation/opioids (naloxone), noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP), or intubation. Treat the underlying cause of hypoventilation.
sections.riskFactors: COPD, respiratory depression from opioids or sedatives, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall disorders, and airway obstruction.

name: Respiratory Alkalosis
shortExplanation: A rise in blood pH from excessive ventilation that blows off too much CO2 (hypocapnia), often from hyperventilation.

sections.presentation: High pH with low PaCO2 on ABG. Signs include lightheadedness, perioral and fingertip numbness/tingling, carpopedal spasm, and anxiety. Often triggered by rapid breathing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause of hyperventilation (anxiety, pain, hypoxemia, sepsis, PE). Reassurance and coached slow breathing help anxiety-driven cases; correct hypoxemia if present.
sections.riskFactors: Anxiety/panic, pain, fever, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, high altitude, pregnancy, and salicylate toxicity.

name: Retinopathy of Prematurity
shortExplanation: Abnormal growth of blood vessels in the eyes of premature infants that, if severe, can lead to retinal detachment and blindness.

sections.presentation: There are no outward symptoms; the condition is found on screening dilated eye exams performed on at-risk preterm infants. Disease is graded by stage and location within the retina.
sections.typicalTreatments: Many mild cases resolve on their own with monitoring. Advanced disease is treated with laser therapy or anti-VEGF injections to prevent retinal detachment. Careful oxygen management helps reduce the risk.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity and low birth weight, prolonged or high supplemental oxygen exposure, and unstable oxygen saturations.

name: Second-Degree AV Block
shortExplanation: Intermittent failure of AV conduction so some P waves do not reach the ventricles; includes Mobitz I (Wenckebach) and the more dangerous Mobitz II.

sections.presentation: Mobitz I shows progressive PR lengthening until a QRS is dropped and is often benign. Mobitz II shows dropped beats without PR prolongation and can progress abruptly to complete block; may cause fatigue, dizziness, or syncope.
sections.typicalTreatments: Mobitz I usually needs only monitoring and medication review. Mobitz II often requires a permanent pacemaker; use atropine cautiously and transcutaneous pacing for symptomatic bradycardia while awaiting a pacemaker.
sections.riskFactors: Myocardial ischemia/infarction (especially inferior for Mobitz I, anterior for Mobitz II), AV-nodal blocking drugs, increased vagal tone, and conduction system disease.

name: Sepsis
shortExplanation: A life-threatening response to infection that can lead to organ dysfunction and shock if not treated quickly.

sections.presentation: Fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension in severe cases (septic shock).
sections.typicalTreatments: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if hypotension persists, source control of the underlying infection.
sections.riskFactors: Immunosuppression, indwelling catheters/lines, recent surgery, advanced age, chronic illness.

name: Septic Shock
shortExplanation: The most severe form of sepsis, where infection causes dangerously low blood pressure and poor organ perfusion that persist despite fluids and require vasopressors.

sections.presentation: Signs of infection plus persistent low blood pressure needing vasopressors to maintain perfusion, an elevated lactate, fever or low temperature, fast heart rate, altered mental status, mottled skin, and low urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Early broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures, IV fluid resuscitation, and vasopressors (norepinephrine first) to maintain a mean arterial pressure goal; source control; and serial lactate measurement following the sepsis bundle.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, immunosuppression, chronic illness, recent surgery or invasive devices, and untreated or severe infection.

name: Serotonin Syndrome
shortExplanation: A potentially life-threatening reaction from too much serotonin activity, usually from combining serotonergic medications.

sections.presentation: A triad of mental status changes (agitation, confusion), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, high blood pressure, sweating, dilated pupils), and neuromuscular abnormalities (tremor, hyperreflexia, and clonus that is often more pronounced in the legs). Onset is usually rapid, within hours of a change in serotonergic drugs.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop all serotonergic agents, provide supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, control agitation and muscle rigidity with benzodiazepines, and use cyproheptadine as a serotonin blocker in more severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, certain opioids like tramadol, triptans, linezolid), overdose, or adding a new serotonergic agent.

name: Small Bowel Obstruction
shortExplanation: A blockage of the small intestine that stops the normal passage of contents, causing pain, vomiting, and distension.

sections.presentation: Crampy abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and inability to pass stool or gas; bowel sounds may be high-pitched then absent.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest (nothing by mouth), a nasogastric tube for decompression, IV fluids, and electrolyte correction. Surgery is needed for strangulation or if it does not resolve.
sections.riskFactors: Prior abdominal surgery (adhesions), hernias, tumors, and Crohn disease.

name: Spinal Cord Injury
shortExplanation: Damage to the spinal cord that causes loss of motor, sensory, or autonomic function below the level of injury. It may be complete or incomplete.

sections.presentation: Weakness or paralysis and sensory loss below the injury level, loss of bowel and bladder control, and possible respiratory compromise with high cervical injuries. Neurogenic shock (hypotension with bradycardia) may occur acutely; later, autonomic dysreflexia can cause dangerous blood pressure spikes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Spinal immobilization and airway protection; maintain perfusion and oxygenation to limit secondary injury; surgical decompression and stabilization as indicated; prevent complications (pressure injury, DVT, respiratory issues); intensive rehabilitation. For autonomic dysreflexia, sit the patient up and remove the trigger (often bladder distension) urgently.
sections.riskFactors: Motor vehicle crashes, falls (especially in older adults), sports injuries, violence, osteoporosis, and conditions narrowing the spinal canal.

name: Status Epilepticus
shortExplanation: A seizure that lasts too long or repeated seizures without full recovery in between - a neurologic emergency that needs immediate treatment.

sections.presentation: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without returning to baseline. Nonconvulsive status may show only altered consciousness and requires EEG to detect.
sections.typicalTreatments: Airway and oxygen support, benzodiazepines as first-line, followed by an antiseizure medication (such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate). Refractory cases may need continuous infusions and intubation. Check and treat glucose and other reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Known epilepsy with missed medication, acute brain injury or stroke, infection, metabolic disturbances, alcohol or drug withdrawal, and low glucose.

name: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
shortExplanation: Bleeding into the space between the brain and its surrounding membranes, most often from a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. It is a neurologic emergency.

sections.presentation: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache often described as the worst of life, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, nausea and vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, seizures, focal deficits. Diagnosed by CT and, if needed, lumbar puncture showing blood or xanthochromia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Secure the aneurysm by surgical clipping or endovascular coiling; nimodipine to reduce vasospasm-related deficits; blood pressure control before securing; monitor for rebleeding, hydrocephalus, and delayed cerebral ischemia. Frequent neuro checks in ICU.
sections.riskFactors: Cerebral aneurysm, hypertension, smoking, heavy alcohol use, family history, polycystic kidney disease, arteriovenous malformation.

name: Subdural Hematoma
shortExplanation: A collection of blood between the dura and the brain surface, usually from torn bridging veins after head trauma. It can develop acutely or slowly over weeks.

sections.presentation: Headache, confusion, drowsiness, focal weakness, unequal pupils, and declining level of consciousness. Chronic subdurals in older or anticoagulated patients may cause gradual cognitive decline or gait changes; acute subdurals present rapidly after trauma.
sections.typicalTreatments: Surgical evacuation (burr holes or craniotomy) for large or symptomatic bleeds; small ones may be observed with serial imaging; reverse anticoagulation; control intracranial pressure and prevent secondary injury.
sections.riskFactors: Head trauma, falls, older age with brain atrophy, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, alcohol misuse, coagulopathy.

name: Surgical Site Infection
shortExplanation: An infection at or near a surgical incision occurring after an operation. It is a common and largely preventable surgical complication.

sections.presentation: Redness, warmth, swelling, increasing pain, and purulent drainage at the incision, sometimes with wound dehiscence and fever. It may be superficial or extend to deep tissue or the organ space.
sections.typicalTreatments: Wound cultures, opening and draining the wound when needed, dressing changes, and antibiotics targeted to the organism. Deep or organ-space infections may need return to the operating room.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes and hyperglycemia, obesity, smoking, prolonged or contaminated surgery, immunosuppression, and lapses in prevention such as mistimed prophylactic antibiotics, hypothermia, or shaving (rather than clipping) the surgical site.

name: Symptomatic Bradycardia
shortExplanation: A heart rate too slow to meet the body's needs — often from a conduction problem (heart block) — causing dizziness, fatigue, or low blood pressure.

sections.presentation: Heart rate typically <60 with symptoms: lightheadedness, fatigue, syncope, hypotension, chest pain, or shortness of breath. ECG may show sinus bradycardia or AV block.
sections.typicalTreatments: Atropine first-line, transcutaneous pacing if atropine fails, dopamine or epinephrine infusion; permanent pacemaker for persistent high-grade block.
sections.riskFactors: Inferior MI, degenerative conduction disease, medications (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin), hyperkalemia, increased vagal tone.

name: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)
shortExplanation: A condition where the body makes too much antidiuretic hormone, causing water retention and dilutional low sodium (hyponatremia).

sections.presentation: Hyponatremia with concentrated urine and a normal-to-slightly-volume-expanded state (euvolemic). Symptoms depend on how low and how fast sodium falls: nausea, headache, confusion, and, when severe, seizures and coma. Low serum osmolality with inappropriately high urine osmolality.
sections.typicalTreatments: Fluid (water) restriction is the mainstay; treat the underlying cause. Severe symptomatic hyponatremia may need hypertonic (3%) saline. Correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination. Vaptans or salt tablets are used in selected cases.
sections.riskFactors: CNS disorders, lung disease, malignancies (especially small-cell lung cancer), medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, others), and surgery or pain.

name: Tension Pneumothorax
shortExplanation: A life-threatening emergency where trapped pleural air progressively builds up, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum to compress the heart and great vessels.

sections.presentation: Severe respiratory distress, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, distended neck veins, hypotension, and tachycardia progressing to cardiac arrest.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate emergency needle decompression (large-bore catheter, typically second intercostal space midclavicular line or fifth intercostal space) followed by chest tube placement. Do not wait for a chest x-ray if unstable.
sections.riskFactors: Chest trauma, positive-pressure mechanical ventilation, CPR, and an untreated simple pneumothorax.

name: Third-Degree (Complete) AV Block
shortExplanation: Total failure of AV conduction where the atria and ventricles beat independently; a slow escape rhythm sustains output and often needs a pacemaker.

sections.presentation: ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes marching out independently (AV dissociation) with a slow ventricular escape rate. Symptoms include fatigue, dizziness, syncope, hypotension, and heart failure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergency transcutaneous pacing for unstable patients (atropine is usually ineffective), followed by a permanent pacemaker. Hold AV-nodal blocking drugs and treat reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Myocardial infarction, degenerative conduction disease, AV-nodal blocking medications, cardiac surgery, and Lyme carditis.

name: Thyroid Storm
shortExplanation: A rare, life-threatening extreme of hyperthyroidism with high fever and severe cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction. A medical emergency.

sections.presentation: High fever, marked tachycardia and often atrial fibrillation, heart failure, agitation, delirium or coma, and GI symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea). Frequently triggered by infection, surgery, trauma, or stopping antithyroid medication.
sections.typicalTreatments: ICU-level care: beta-blockers to control heart rate, antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil or methimazole), iodine given after the antithyroid drug to block hormone release, corticosteroids, aggressive cooling and fluids, and treating the trigger.
sections.riskFactors: Untreated or undertreated hyperthyroidism plus a precipitant such as infection, surgery, trauma, or iodine load.

name: Transient Ischemic Attack
shortExplanation: A brief episode of stroke-like symptoms from temporary loss of blood flow to the brain, resolving without permanent infarction. It is a warning sign of high stroke risk.

sections.presentation: Sudden focal deficits that fully resolve, typically within an hour: unilateral weakness or numbness, facial droop, slurred speech, vision loss, or difficulty speaking. No lasting infarct on imaging.
sections.typicalTreatments: Urgent workup to find the cause (carotid imaging, ECG for atrial fibrillation, labs); antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel) or anticoagulation if cardioembolic; statin, blood pressure and diabetes control; carotid revascularization if indicated.
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, carotid stenosis, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia, prior TIA or stroke, older age.

name: Traumatic Brain Injury
shortExplanation: Brain dysfunction caused by an external force such as a blow or jolt to the head. Severity ranges from mild concussion to life-threatening injury.

sections.presentation: Ranges from brief confusion, headache, and dizziness (mild/concussion) to loss of consciousness, unequal pupils, vomiting, seizures, and coma (severe). Watch for signs of rising intracranial pressure and secondary deterioration. Graded with the Glasgow Coma Scale.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prevent secondary injury by maintaining oxygenation and cerebral perfusion; manage intracranial pressure (head-of-bed elevation, osmotic therapy such as mannitol or hypertonic saline, sedation, and sometimes surgery); frequent neuro assessments; seizure prophylaxis in select cases.
sections.riskFactors: Falls, motor vehicle crashes, assaults, sports and combat injuries, older age, alcohol use, anticoagulation.

name: Tuberculosis
shortExplanation: A bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that primarily affects the lungs and spreads through the air. It exists as latent (inactive) and active disease.

sections.presentation: Active pulmonary TB: chronic productive cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Latent TB has no symptoms and is not contagious. Diagnosed with skin (TST) or blood (IGRA) tests, chest imaging, and sputum studies.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged multidrug regimens (commonly isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for months, often with directly observed therapy; latent TB is treated to prevent progression; airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room for suspected active pulmonary disease.
sections.riskFactors: Close contact with an active case, HIV or immunocompromise, birth or travel in high-prevalence regions, crowded or congregate living, injection drug use, and diabetes.

name: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
shortExplanation: A metabolic emergency in which rapidly dying cancer cells dump their contents into the blood, usually just after starting treatment. The released chemicals can cause dangerous electrolyte swings, kidney failure, and arrhythmias.

sections.presentation: High potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid, and low calcium, leading to nausea, weakness, muscle cramps, tetany, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and acute kidney injury with reduced urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV hydration, close monitoring of electrolytes and kidney function, uric-acid-lowering therapy with allopurinol or rasburicase, and treatment of hyperkalemia. Cardiac monitoring and, in severe cases, dialysis.
sections.riskFactors: Bulky, rapidly proliferating, treatment-sensitive cancers such as acute leukemias and high-grade lymphomas, high tumor burden, pre-existing kidney impairment, and the initiation of chemotherapy.

name: Ulcerative Colitis
shortExplanation: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colon lining, starting at the rectum. Marked by bloody diarrhea.

sections.presentation: Bloody diarrhea with mucus, urgency and tenesmus, crampy lower abdominal pain, and weight loss. Severe flares cause fever and dehydration. Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication. Inflammation is continuous and limited to the colon and rectum.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aminosalicylates (5-ASA) for maintenance, corticosteroids for flares, immunomodulators, and biologics. Colectomy can be curative for refractory disease or complications. Monitor stool frequency, bleeding, and hydration; long-standing disease raises colon cancer risk requiring surveillance.
sections.riskFactors: Family history and age (often diagnosed in young adulthood); risk of colorectal cancer increases with disease duration and extent.

name: Upper GI Bleed
shortExplanation: Bleeding from the upper digestive tract (esophagus, stomach, or duodenum) that can range from minor to life-threatening hemorrhage.

sections.presentation: Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools (melena), and with brisk bleeding, red blood per rectum. Large losses cause lightheadedness, fast heart rate, low blood pressure, and pallor.
sections.typicalTreatments: Large-bore IV access and fluid or blood resuscitation, proton pump inhibitor therapy, and urgent endoscopy to find and control the source. Octreotide and antibiotics for suspected variceal bleeding; transfusion guided by a restrictive strategy for most patients.
sections.riskFactors: Peptic ulcer disease, NSAID or anticoagulant use, H. pylori infection, liver disease with varices, and heavy alcohol use.

name: Urinary Tract Infection
shortExplanation: An infection of the bladder or kidneys; it is a very common reason for admission and can progress to life-threatening urosepsis.

sections.presentation: Burning with urination, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine. Flank pain and fever suggest a kidney infection (pyelonephritis); older adults may show new confusion.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics guided by urine culture, hydration, and removing or changing indwelling catheters when possible.
sections.riskFactors: Female anatomy, indwelling urinary catheters, urinary retention, diabetes, older age, and immobility.

name: Venous Stasis Ulcer
shortExplanation: A chronic lower-leg wound caused by poor vein circulation, and the most common type of leg ulcer.

sections.presentation: Shallow, irregular wounds around the ankle or inner lower leg, with surrounding brown-stained (hemosiderin) and swollen skin; usually mild pain but moderate to heavy drainage.
sections.typicalTreatments: Compression therapy is the cornerstone once adequate arterial flow is confirmed, along with leg elevation, moist wound dressings, and skin care.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic venous insufficiency, prior DVT, obesity, prolonged standing, and older age.

name: Ventricular Fibrillation
shortExplanation: The ventricles quiver chaotically instead of pumping, so there's no effective heartbeat — a form of cardiac arrest that requires immediate CPR and defibrillation.

sections.presentation: Sudden loss of pulse and consciousness; ECG shows disorganized, irregular waveforms with no identifiable QRS complexes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate high-quality CPR and defibrillation (a shockable rhythm), epinephrine and amiodarone per ACLS, and treatment of reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Acute MI/ischemia, cardiomyopathy, severe electrolyte imbalance, prolonged QT, prior cardiac arrest.

name: Ventricular Tachycardia
shortExplanation: A fast rhythm arising from the ventricles — it can be stable, or become pulseless and life-threatening. Treatment depends on whether the patient has a pulse and is stable.

sections.presentation: Palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness; may deteriorate to loss of pulse. ECG shows a wide-complex, regular, fast rhythm.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pulseless VT: CPR and defibrillation per ACLS. Unstable with a pulse: synchronized cardioversion. Stable: antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone.
sections.riskFactors: Prior MI/scar, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte abnormalities, prolonged QT, structural heart disease.

name: Viral Hepatitis
shortExplanation: Liver inflammation caused by hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, E). A and E spread through contaminated food/water; B, C, and D spread through blood and body fluids.

sections.presentation: Fatigue, nausea, poor appetite, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. Elevated liver enzymes. Hepatitis A and E are usually acute and self-limited; B and C can become chronic and lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supportive care for acute infection. Chronic hepatitis B and C are treated with antiviral medications; hepatitis C is often curable with direct-acting antivirals. Vaccination prevents hepatitis A and B. Use standard precautions and avoid hepatotoxins such as alcohol.
sections.riskFactors: Injection drug use, unprotected sex, needlestick exposure, contaminated food or water (A and E), and perinatal transmission (B).

name: 12-Lead ECG
shortExplanation: A recording of the heart's electrical activity from 12 angles — the key bedside test for diagnosing a heart attack and identifying arrhythmias.

sections.purpose: Capture a detailed electrical snapshot of the heart to detect ischemia/infarction, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and electrolyte effects.
sections.careConsiderations: Place limb and precordial leads in correct anatomic positions (misplacement mimics pathology); prep skin for a clean signal; minimize motion artifact; get it within 10 minutes for chest pain and compare with prior tracings.

name: BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure)
shortExplanation: A noninvasive ventilation device that delivers two pressure levels - higher on inhalation and lower on exhalation - to support breathing without intubation.

sections.purpose: Provides a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) to assist breaths and a lower expiratory pressure (EPAP) to keep alveoli open. Used for COPD exacerbations with CO2 retention, acute heart failure, and to avoid intubation in respiratory failure.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm the patient is awake enough to protect the airway; avoid in patients unable to clear secretions or at high aspiration risk. Monitor ABGs, mental status, respiratory rate, and mask fit. Watch for gastric distension, aspiration, and facial pressure injury; be ready to escalate to intubation if the patient worsens.

name: Bladder Scanner
shortExplanation: A portable ultrasound device that noninvasively measures the volume of urine in the bladder.

sections.purpose: Estimates bladder volume and post-void residual to evaluate urinary retention, decide whether catheterization is needed, and avoid unnecessary catheter insertions that risk infection.
sections.careConsiderations: Position the patient supine, apply gel, and aim toward the pubic bone for an accurate reading. Select the correct sex/gender setting; a prior hysterectomy affects the setting. A large post-void residual may prompt intermittent catheterization per protocol rather than an indwelling catheter.

name: Blood Glucose Meter (Glucometer)
shortExplanation: A handheld device that measures blood sugar from a drop of capillary blood at the bedside.

sections.purpose: Gives a rapid point-of-care glucose reading to guide insulin dosing, catch hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, and monitor diabetic and critically ill patients.
sections.careConsiderations: Use control solutions and quality checks per policy, and confirm the test strips are not expired. Cleanse the site, wipe away the first drop if needy, and use the side of the fingertip. Very high or very low readings, or values that do not fit the patient, should be confirmed with a venous lab sample before major treatment.

name: Capnography Monitor
shortExplanation: A monitor that measures exhaled carbon dioxide (end-tidal CO2) breath by breath, used to confirm airway placement and watch breathing in real time.

sections.purpose: Continuously measure end-tidal CO2 to confirm and monitor endotracheal tube placement, detect early respiratory depression during sedation, and assess ventilation and the effectiveness of CPR.
sections.careConsiderations: Recognize the normal waveform and values (end-tidal CO2 roughly 35-45 mmHg). A sudden loss of waveform can mean a dislodged tube, disconnection, or cardiac arrest. During procedural sedation it detects hypoventilation earlier than pulse oximetry. Keep the sensor free of secretions and moisture.

name: Cardiac Telemetry Monitor
shortExplanation: Continuous wireless heart-rhythm monitoring that lets staff watch for arrhythmias in real time from a central station.

sections.purpose: Continuously track heart rhythm and rate to catch arrhythmias, ischemic changes, or dangerous rate changes early.
sections.careConsiderations: Place and change electrodes on clean, dry skin; know each patient's alarm parameters and respond to alarms (avoid alarm fatigue); ensure leads stay connected and the battery is charged; correlate any rhythm change with the patient's symptoms and a 12-lead ECG.

name: Central Venous Catheter (Device)
shortExplanation: A catheter whose tip sits in a large central vein, used for medications, fluids, and monitoring that a peripheral IV cannot handle.

sections.purpose: Provides reliable access for vesicant or irritating drugs (vasopressors, chemotherapy, TPN), rapid large-volume resuscitation, central venous pressure monitoring, and long-term therapy. Types include internal jugular/subclavian lines, PICCs, and tunneled catheters and ports.
sections.careConsiderations: Follow strict sterile technique and central-line bundle practices to prevent CLABSI: scrub the hub, keep the dressing clean/dry/occlusive, and remove the line as soon as it is no longer needed. Assess the site for redness or drainage, confirm blood return before use, and watch for air embolism when caps or tubing are open.

name: Chest Drainage System (Pleur-evac)
shortExplanation: A closed collection system connected to a chest tube that drains air, blood, or fluid from the pleural space and prevents it from re-entering.

sections.purpose: Uses a three-chamber design - collection, water seal, and suction control - to evacuate air or fluid, re-expand the lung, and restore negative pleural pressure after pneumothorax, hemothorax, effusion, or thoracic surgery.
sections.careConsiderations: Keep the unit upright and below chest level. Assess for tidaling in the water-seal chamber (normal) and continuous bubbling (indicates an air leak or loose connection). Monitor drainage amount, color, and rate; report sudden increases in bright red drainage. Never clamp the tube routinely; if it disconnects, place the end in sterile water. Keep an occlusive dressing and clamp at the bedside.

name: CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure)
shortExplanation: A noninvasive device that delivers one constant level of positive airway pressure to keep the airways and alveoli open.

sections.purpose: Maintains a single continuous pressure throughout the breathing cycle, splinting open the upper airway and alveoli. Used chiefly for obstructive sleep apnea and to improve oxygenation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure a good mask seal without excessive tightness; watch for pressure injury on the nose bridge and facial skin. Monitor for gastric distension, aspiration risk, and claustrophobia. The patient must be able to protect their own airway and breathe spontaneously.

name: Defibrillator
shortExplanation: The device that delivers a shock to the heart — used unsynchronized to defibrillate arrest rhythms, or synchronized to cardiovert unstable ones; many also pace.

sections.purpose: Deliver a controlled electrical shock to terminate life-threatening arrhythmias (defibrillation for VF/pulseless VT; synchronized cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias) and provide transcutaneous pacing.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure pads have good skin contact and clear everyone before discharge ("I'm clear, you're clear"); select sync mode for cardioversion but not for defibrillation; keep it charged and checked each shift; remove medication patches and avoid pad placement over an implanted device.

name: Enteral Feeding Pump
shortExplanation: A pump that delivers tube feeding formula at a controlled rate through a feeding tube.

sections.purpose: Delivers enteral nutrition at a set rate (continuous, cyclic, or bolus) through a nasogastric, PEG, or other feeding tube for patients who cannot eat safely by mouth.
sections.careConsiderations: Keep the head of bed elevated at least 30-45 degrees to reduce aspiration risk. Verify tube placement and check residuals per policy, flush the tube to prevent clogging, and use only enteral (ENFit) connectors so tube feeding can never be connected to an IV line.

name: Enteral Feeding Tube (Device)
shortExplanation: A tube placed into the stomach or small intestine to deliver nutrition, fluids, and medication when a patient cannot eat safely.

sections.purpose: Provides a route for enteral nutrition and medications. Short-term options include nasogastric and nasojejunal tubes; long-term options include surgically or endoscopically placed gastrostomy (PEG) and jejunostomy tubes.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm placement before use per policy (initial x-ray for new NG tubes; check external length and markings before each feed). Flush before and after feeds and medications to prevent clogs, give medications in liquid form when possible, and keep the head of bed elevated to reduce aspiration. Assess the insertion or stoma site for skin breakdown.

name: High-Flow Nasal Cannula
shortExplanation: A system delivering heated, humidified oxygen at high flow rates through wide nasal prongs, providing precise FiO2 and some positive airway pressure.

sections.purpose: Delivers up to 60 L/min of warmed, humidified gas with an adjustable FiO2 up to 100 percent, generating a small amount of PEEP and washing out CO2. Used for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure as an alternative to noninvasive ventilation.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure the water chamber and heated circuit are working so gas is well humidified. Monitor SpO2, work of breathing, and respiratory rate closely; escalate to noninvasive ventilation or intubation if the patient tires. Keep prongs correctly sized and check nares for pressure injury.

name: Home Oxygen Therapy
shortExplanation: Supplemental oxygen delivered in the home for patients with chronic low blood oxygen, such as those with advanced COPD or heart failure. It is usually supplied by a concentrator or portable tanks.

sections.purpose: Maintains adequate blood oxygen levels to reduce breathlessness, support organ function, and improve activity tolerance and survival in patients with chronic hypoxemia.
sections.careConsiderations: Deliver oxygen at the prescribed flow through nasal cannula or mask; do not change the rate without an order, since some patients rely on a lower drive to breathe. Teach fire safety strictly (no smoking, flames, or heat sources near oxygen, since it strongly supports combustion), secure tubing to prevent falls, provide skin and nasal care to prevent breakdown, humidify at higher flows, and have a backup plan and supplier contact for equipment or power failure.

name: Implanted Port
shortExplanation: A small device placed under the skin, usually on the chest, connected to a catheter in a large central vein. It gives durable access for chemotherapy, blood draws, and infusions, and is accessed with a special non-coring needle.

sections.purpose: Provides reliable, long-term central venous access for repeated chemotherapy, infusions, transfusions, and blood sampling, sparing peripheral veins and reducing the risk of vesicant extravasation when used correctly.
sections.careConsiderations: Access with a non-coring (Huber) needle using sterile technique, confirm blood return before infusing, and flush per protocol (often with saline and sometimes heparin) to keep it patent. Monitor for infection at the site or bloodstream, occlusion, catheter migration, and (rarely) the needle dislodging from the port during infusion of a vesicant. Teach the patient the signs of infection and how the port is used.

name: Incentive Spirometer
shortExplanation: A handheld breathing device that encourages slow, deep breaths to keep the lungs expanded after surgery or during immobility.

sections.purpose: Promotes deep breathing to prevent atelectasis (collapsed air sacs) and reduce the risk of pneumonia after surgery or with limited mobility.
sections.careConsiderations: Teach the patient to inhale slowly and deeply, hold a few seconds, and aim for a target volume, roughly 10 times per hour while awake. Provide it after pain is controlled and have the patient splint incisions with a pillow when coughing.

name: Indwelling Urinary Catheter (Device)
shortExplanation: A Foley catheter that stays in the bladder with a small inflated balloon to drain urine continuously.

sections.purpose: Continuously drains the bladder for urinary retention, close monitoring of output in critical illness, perioperative needs, or comfort in select situations. A balloon holds it in place and urine collects in a drainage bag.
sections.careConsiderations: Because it is the leading cause of hospital urinary infections (CAUTI), keep it only as long as truly needed and remove it early. Maintain a closed system, keep the bag below bladder level and off the floor, secure the tubing to prevent traction, and perform routine perineal care. Assess for output, obstruction, and signs of infection.

name: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump
shortExplanation: A balloon in the aorta that inflates and deflates with the heartbeat to boost coronary blood flow and ease the heart's workload — used in severe heart failure or cardiogenic shock.

sections.purpose: Provide temporary mechanical circulatory support — inflating in diastole to improve coronary perfusion and deflating in systole to reduce afterload, increasing cardiac output.
sections.careConsiderations: Verify timing to the cardiac cycle (inflation on the dicrotic notch), keep the affected leg straight and monitor distal pulses/perfusion, watch the insertion site for bleeding, monitor platelets and for limb/renal ischemia, and never let the balloon sit idle (clot risk).

name: IV Infusion Pump
shortExplanation: An electronic pump that delivers IV fluids and medications at a precise, programmed rate.

sections.purpose: Delivers a controlled volume of fluid or medication over time, allowing accurate titration of drips such as vasopressors, heparin, and insulin. Smart pumps include drug libraries with dose limits ('guardrails') to catch programming errors.
sections.careConsiderations: Verify the drug, concentration, rate, and channel against the order at the pump. Watch for occlusion, air-in-line, and infiltration alarms and troubleshoot promptly. Trace each line from bag to patient before changing settings, and label lines to avoid mix-ups with multiple infusions.

name: Mechanical Ventilator
shortExplanation: A machine that delivers breaths through a breathing tube to support or fully take over a patient's breathing when they cannot breathe adequately on their own.

sections.purpose: Support or replace spontaneous breathing by delivering controlled oxygen and pressure, ensuring adequate oxygenation and carbon dioxide removal in respiratory failure, during sedation and paralysis, or after major surgery.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm tube placement and secure it, monitor settings (mode, tidal volume, rate, FiO2, PEEP) and alarms, and respond promptly to high-pressure or low-pressure alarms. Provide oral care and elevate the head of the bed to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia, manage sedation to a goal, and assess readiness for weaning with spontaneous breathing trials.

name: Nasal Cannula
shortExplanation: A lightweight two-pronged tube that delivers low-flow supplemental oxygen through the nostrils; the most common oxygen device.

sections.purpose: Delivers low-flow oxygen, typically 1-6 L/min, providing roughly 24-44 percent FiO2. Comfortable and allows eating and talking, making it ideal for stable patients needing modest oxygen.
sections.careConsiderations: Delivered FiO2 varies with the patient's breathing pattern. Check ears, cheeks, and nostrils for skin breakdown and pad tubing as needed. Humidify flows above about 4 L/min to reduce nasal drying. Ensure prongs curve downward into the nares.

name: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy
shortExplanation: A wound vacuum system that applies gentle suction through a sealed dressing to speed healing of complex wounds.

sections.purpose: A sealed foam or gauze dressing connected to suction removes wound fluid, reduces swelling, and stimulates granulation tissue, helping deep or chronic wounds heal.
sections.careConsiderations: Maintain an airtight seal and the prescribed suction level; monitor canister output and change the dressing per protocol. Watch for bleeding (it should not be placed over exposed vessels or organs) and protect the skin around the seal.

name: Non-Rebreather Mask
shortExplanation: A high-concentration oxygen mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves used for critically ill or severely hypoxemic patients.

sections.purpose: Delivers the highest oxygen concentration of the standard masks (up to about 90-95 percent FiO2) at 10-15 L/min, used for acute hypoxemia, trauma, and pre-oxygenation.
sections.careConsiderations: Set flow high enough to keep the reservoir bag inflated (never let it fully collapse on inspiration). One-way valves prevent rebreathing of exhaled air. Reassess frequently; a patient still hypoxemic on a non-rebreather may need noninvasive ventilation or intubation.

name: Oropharyngeal Airway (OPA)
shortExplanation: A rigid curved device inserted into the mouth to hold the tongue away from the back of the throat and keep the airway open in an unconscious patient.

sections.purpose: Prevents the tongue from obstructing the airway in an unresponsive patient without a gag reflex, aiding bag-mask ventilation. A nasopharyngeal airway is the alternative used when a gag reflex is present.
sections.careConsiderations: Use only in patients without a gag reflex; it can trigger gagging, vomiting, and aspiration or laryngospasm in responsive patients. Size by measuring from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe/angle of the jaw. Reassess airway patency and remove if the patient regains a gag reflex.

name: Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) Pump
shortExplanation: An infusion pump that lets a patient self-administer preset doses of IV pain medication by pressing a button.

sections.purpose: Gives the patient control over analgesia (commonly morphine, hydromorphone, or fentanyl) with programmed dose, lockout interval, and hourly limits, improving pain control while limiting overdose.
sections.careConsiderations: Only the patient should press the button - warn family against 'PCA by proxy.' Monitor sedation level, respiratory rate, and pulse oximetry (and capnography per policy) because oversedation is the main danger. Verify pump settings with a second nurse, and keep naloxone available.

name: Peak Flow Meter
shortExplanation: A handheld device that measures peak expiratory flow rate to monitor asthma control and detect worsening airway obstruction.

sections.purpose: Measures how fast a patient can forcefully exhale (peak expiratory flow), reflecting airway narrowing. Used at home to track asthma control and guide an asthma action plan (green/yellow/red zones based on personal best).
sections.careConsiderations: Teach a full deep breath and a fast, hard blow while standing, taking the best of three attempts. Establish the patient's personal best when well. A falling peak flow can warn of an exacerbation before symptoms worsen, prompting action-plan steps.

name: Pulse Oximeter
shortExplanation: A noninvasive sensor, usually clipped to a finger, that estimates blood oxygen saturation and heart rate.

sections.purpose: Continuously or intermittently measures oxygen saturation (SpO2) to detect hypoxemia and guide oxygen therapy. It is a core vital sign on nearly every unit.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure a good waveform or signal; poor perfusion, motion, cold digits, and nail polish cause false readings. It cannot detect carbon monoxide poisoning (falsely normal) and may read less accurately at low saturations and on darker skin tones. Correlate a surprising value with the patient's clinical picture before acting.

name: Pulse Oximetry
shortExplanation: A noninvasive sensor that estimates blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate by shining light through a fingertip, toe, or earlobe.

sections.purpose: Provides continuous or spot-check measurement of oxygen saturation, allowing rapid detection of hypoxemia and titration of oxygen therapy. Normal SpO2 is generally 95-100 percent (often 88-92 percent target in chronic CO2 retainers).
sections.careConsiderations: Accuracy is reduced by poor perfusion, motion, nail polish, cold extremities, and severe anemia. It cannot detect carbon monoxide poisoning (falsely normal) and does not measure ventilation/CO2. Rotate probe sites to prevent skin/pressure injury and correlate readings with the patient's clinical picture and, when needed, an ABG.

name: Sequential Compression Device (SCD)
shortExplanation: Inflatable leg sleeves that squeeze the calves in a cycle to promote venous return and prevent blood clots.

sections.purpose: Provides mechanical prophylaxis against deep vein thrombosis in immobile or postoperative patients by mimicking the calf muscle pump and reducing venous stasis. Used alone when anticoagulation is contraindicated, or with it for higher-risk patients.
sections.careConsiderations: Apply correctly sized sleeves and keep them on except during ambulation, hygiene, and skin checks. Assess skin and neurovascular status, and do not apply over an existing DVT or ischemic limb. Reinforce that they only work when actually worn and connected.

name: Simple Face Mask
shortExplanation: A soft mask covering the nose and mouth that delivers moderate-concentration oxygen at medium flow rates.

sections.purpose: Delivers roughly 40-60 percent FiO2 at flows of about 5-10 L/min for patients needing more oxygen than a nasal cannula provides.
sections.careConsiderations: Keep flow at least 5-6 L/min to flush exhaled CO2 from the mask and prevent rebreathing. Watch for skin breakdown at the ears, nose bridge, and cheeks. The mask must be removed for eating and drinking, so plan care around it.

name: Venturi Mask
shortExplanation: A high-flow oxygen mask with color-coded adapters that delivers a precise, fixed oxygen concentration regardless of the patient's breathing.

sections.purpose: Delivers an exact FiO2 (commonly 24-50 percent) using interchangeable color-coded valves. Preferred when precise, controlled oxygen is needed, such as in COPD patients at risk of CO2 retention.
sections.careConsiderations: Match the correct adapter and flow rate to the ordered FiO2 (each color specifies a flow). Keep the air-entrainment ports unobstructed. Remove for meals and monitor SpO2 and, in CO2 retainers, watch for rising drowsiness or CO2 retention.

name: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
shortExplanation: A clotting test of the intrinsic and common pathways, most often used to monitor unfractionated heparin.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 25-35 seconds (lab dependent).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Prolonged aPTT is seen with heparin therapy, hemophilia, clotting-factor deficiencies, and lupus anticoagulant. When titrating a heparin drip, the goal aPTT is set by protocol. It is often ordered alongside PT/INR to evaluate bleeding.

name: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)
shortExplanation: A liver enzyme that is more specific to the liver than AST and rises with liver-cell injury.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 7-56 U/L.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high ALT is a fairly specific sign of liver injury from viral hepatitis, medications (including acetaminophen toxicity), alcohol, or fatty liver disease. It is trended with AST, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase to distinguish liver-cell injury from bile-duct obstruction.

name: Albumin
shortExplanation: The main protein in blood; low levels can flag malnutrition or illness and are linked to poor wound healing.

sections.normalRange: About 3.5-5.0 g/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low albumin can reflect malnutrition, inflammation, liver disease, or protein loss through the kidneys or gut, and is associated with poor wound healing and edema. It is a marker of nutrition and overall illness rather than a specific diagnosis.

name: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
shortExplanation: An enzyme found mainly in the liver's bile ducts and in bone; useful for detecting bile-duct and bone disease.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 44-147 U/L in adults (higher in growing children and pregnancy).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high ALP suggests bile-duct obstruction (cholestasis) or bone disorders such as Paget disease and bony metastases. Checking GGT helps tell whether the source is liver or bone. Physiologic elevation is normal in growing children and in pregnancy.

name: Ammonia
shortExplanation: A blood test of a nitrogen waste product that can build up when the liver fails to clear it, contributing to confusion in hepatic encephalopathy.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 15-45 mcg/dL in adults, though reference ranges vary by laboratory and method.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels are associated with hepatic encephalopathy and other causes of impaired ammonia clearance. The level does not always correlate tightly with the degree of confusion, so treatment is guided mainly by the clinical picture. Proper sample handling (kept on ice and processed promptly) is important because delays falsely raise results.

name: Anion Gap
shortExplanation: A calculated value from the metabolic panel used to work out the cause of a metabolic acidosis.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 8-12 mEq/L (varies by lab and whether potassium is included).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high anion gap points to acidosis from accumulated acids - classic causes include DKA, lactic acidosis, kidney failure, and toxic ingestions. A normal-gap acidosis is more typical of bicarbonate loss such as diarrhea. It is calculated as sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate.

name: Arterial Blood Gas
shortExplanation: A blood test drawn from an artery that measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acid-base balance to assess how well the lungs and metabolism are working.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low pH is acidosis, high pH is alkalosis. A high PaCO2 points to respiratory acidosis (inadequate ventilation); a low PaCO2 to respiratory alkalosis. Abnormal HCO3 reflects metabolic disturbances. Low PaO2 or SaO2 indicates hypoxemia. Results guide ventilator settings and treatment of acid-base disorders.

name: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
shortExplanation: A liver enzyme (also found in heart and muscle) that rises when those tissues are injured.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 10-40 U/L.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated AST indicates liver-cell injury from hepatitis, alcohol, medications, or fatty liver, but because AST is also in muscle and heart, it can rise with muscle injury. It is interpreted alongside ALT; an AST:ALT ratio above 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease.

name: Blood Cultures
shortExplanation: A test that grows and identifies bacteria or fungi in the blood to diagnose bloodstream infection and guide antibiotic choice. Proper collection is key to accurate results.

sections.normalRange: No growth (negative) after incubation. Results are qualitative rather than a numeric range.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A positive culture indicates organisms in the blood (bacteremia or fungemia), supporting diagnoses such as sepsis, endocarditis, or line infection, and guides targeted therapy. A single positive with a common skin organism may reflect contamination. Draw before starting antibiotics when possible, using proper skin antisepsis, and collect at least two sets from separate sites; report results promptly so therapy can be tailored.

name: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
shortExplanation: A blood test reflecting kidney function and hydration; it measures a nitrogen waste product from protein breakdown.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 7-20 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High with kidney impairment, dehydration, GI bleeding, high protein intake, or tissue breakdown; low with overhydration or liver disease. It is interpreted alongside creatinine, and the BUN-to-creatinine ratio helps identify dehydration-related (prerenal) causes.

name: BNP
shortExplanation: A hormone released when the heart's chambers are stretched by fluid overload — helps confirm and gauge the severity of heart failure.

sections.normalRange: Typically <100 pg/mL for BNP; NT-proBNP cutoffs are higher and rise with age. Interpreted alongside the clinical picture.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels suggest cardiac wall stretch from heart failure/volume overload; higher values generally mean more severe decompensation. Levels can also rise with renal dysfunction and are lower in obesity.

name: C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
shortExplanation: A blood marker of inflammation that rises with infection, tissue injury, and inflammatory disease. It is used to detect and monitor inflammation over time.

sections.normalRange: Generally less than about 10 mg/L (roughly under 1 mg/dL) in healthy adults; high-sensitivity CRP is reported in lower ranges for cardiovascular risk. Reference values vary by lab and assay.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated CRP indicates inflammation from infection, autoimmune disease, tissue injury, or other causes; it is sensitive but not specific. Rising or persistently high levels can suggest worsening or uncontrolled infection, while falling levels often indicate response to treatment. Interpret alongside the clinical picture and other markers such as ESR and procalcitonin.

name: Central Venous Oxygen Saturation
shortExplanation: The oxygen saturation of blood returning through a central line, used as a marker of the balance between oxygen delivery and how much tissue is using.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 65-70% or higher for ScvO2 measured from a central venous catheter.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A low value suggests oxygen delivery is not keeping up with demand - from low cardiac output, anemia, hypoxemia, or increased consumption - as seen in shock. An unusually high value can reflect impaired oxygen extraction by tissues, as in some cases of septic shock. Trends help guide resuscitation.

name: CK-MB
shortExplanation: The heart-associated fraction of creatine kinase; historically used to detect heart-muscle injury, now largely replaced by troponin.

sections.normalRange: Generally 0-3 ng/mL, or under about 5% of total CK (assay dependent).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A rise in CK-MB indicates heart-muscle injury, as in myocardial infarction. Because it clears faster than troponin, it was once used to detect reinfarction, but troponin is now the preferred cardiac marker. Skeletal muscle injury can also raise CK-MB modestly.

name: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
shortExplanation: A common panel measuring the red cells, white cells, and platelets to screen for infection, anemia, and bleeding risk.

sections.normalRange: Includes white blood cells (about 4.5-11 x10^9/L), hemoglobin (about 12-16 g/dL in women and 13.5-17.5 in men), hematocrit, and platelets (about 150-400 x10^9/L).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high white count suggests infection or inflammation and a low count suggests marrow suppression; low hemoglobin and hematocrit indicate anemia or blood loss; low platelets raise bleeding risk.

name: Cortisol
shortExplanation: The body's main stress hormone, made by the adrenal glands. Blood levels are measured to evaluate adrenal and pituitary disorders.

sections.normalRange: Levels follow a daily rhythm, highest in the early morning and lowest at night, so timing matters. Reference ranges vary by lab and by the time of the draw; dynamic tests (such as ACTH stimulation) are often needed for diagnosis.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low cortisol suggests adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) or pituitary failure and can indicate risk of adrenal crisis. High cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome (from tumors or steroid medication) or acute stress. Because of the daily rhythm and stress effects, single random values are interpreted cautiously and often confirmed with stimulation or suppression testing.

name: Creatine Kinase (CK)
shortExplanation: An enzyme released when muscle is damaged; a marker of muscle injury including rhabdomyolysis.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 30-200 U/L (varies by sex, race, and muscle mass).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Very high CK indicates muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) from crush injury, prolonged immobility, seizures, intense exertion, or statins, and threatens the kidneys. Milder elevations occur after IM injections or strenuous activity. Trend CK and protect kidneys with fluids when it is markedly high.

name: Creatinine
shortExplanation: A blood waste product filtered by the kidneys; it is the main marker used to track kidney function.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0.6-1.2 mg/dL, varying with muscle mass, sex, and age.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A rising creatinine indicates worsening kidney function and is used to estimate the GFR for staging kidney disease. Low values usually reflect low muscle mass.

name: D-dimer
shortExplanation: A blood marker of clot breakdown used mainly to help rule out venous clots when suspicion is low.

sections.normalRange: Typically negative below about 500 ng/mL FEU (assay dependent; some labs use age-adjusted cutoffs).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A negative D-dimer in a low-risk patient helps rule out DVT or PE. An elevated D-dimer is nonspecific - it rises with clots but also with infection, surgery, trauma, pregnancy, and advanced age - so a positive result usually prompts imaging rather than confirming a clot.

name: Digoxin Level
shortExplanation: A blood level checked to keep digoxin in its narrow safe range — too high risks toxicity and dangerous arrhythmias.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0.5–2.0 ng/mL, with lower targets (about 0.5–0.9) often preferred in heart failure. Drawn at least 6 hours after the dose.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels (worsened by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and renal impairment) point to toxicity — nausea, visual changes, and arrhythmias. Interpret alongside symptoms and potassium.

name: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
shortExplanation: A blood test that measures how quickly red blood cells settle, serving as a nonspecific marker of inflammation. It changes more slowly than CRP.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 0 to 15 mm/hr in adult men and 0 to 20 mm/hr in adult women; values rise with age and vary by lab. Often summarized with the Westergren method.
sections.abnormalMeaning: An elevated ESR reflects inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, or certain malignancies but is nonspecific and rises and falls gradually. It is useful for conditions such as osteomyelitis, temporal arteritis, and polymyalgia rheumatica and for monitoring disease activity over time. Interpret together with CRP and the clinical context; very high values warrant further evaluation.

name: Ferritin
shortExplanation: A blood protein that stores iron; ferritin is the best single marker of the body's iron stores.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 12-300 ng/mL (varies by sex and lab; lower in menstruating women).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low ferritin confirms iron-deficiency anemia. High ferritin can mean iron overload but is also an acute-phase reactant, rising with infection, inflammation, and liver disease, so a normal or high ferritin does not fully exclude iron deficiency in an ill patient.

name: Fibrinogen
shortExplanation: A clotting protein (factor I) that forms the fibrin mesh of a clot; a key value in bleeding and DIC.

sections.normalRange: About 200-400 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low fibrinogen occurs with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), massive hemorrhage, and severe liver disease and increases bleeding risk; it may be replaced with cryoprecipitate. As an acute-phase reactant, fibrinogen also rises with inflammation and pregnancy.

name: Free Thyroxine (Free T4)
shortExplanation: The active, unbound form of the thyroid hormone thyroxine in the blood. Used with TSH to assess thyroid function.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 0.8-1.8 ng/dL in adults (reference ranges vary by laboratory).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A low free T4 with a high TSH confirms primary hypothyroidism. A high free T4 with a low TSH confirms hyperthyroidism. Free T4 helps distinguish primary from central thyroid disorders and gauges severity when interpreting an abnormal TSH.

name: Glucose
shortExplanation: Blood sugar level — closely monitored in patients with diabetes, on insulin therapy, or during critical illness.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 70–100 mg/dL fasting; targets differ for hospitalized/critically ill patients and vary by institution protocol.
