sections.targetConcern: Severe multi-vessel or left main coronary disease that isn't well suited to stenting, often with angina or reduced heart function.
sections.whatToMonitor: Hemodynamics and cardiac rhythm (arrhythmias are common postoperatively), chest tube output, sternal incision and graft harvest sites for bleeding/infection, respiratory status and pain control, neuro status after bypass.

name: Defibrillation
shortExplanation: An unsynchronized electrical shock delivered to a pulseless, chaotic rhythm (VF or pulseless VT) to stop it and give the heart a chance to restart a normal rhythm.

sections.targetConcern: Ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia — a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation.
sections.whatToMonitor: Rhythm and pulse immediately after each shock, quality of CPR between shocks, airway and oxygenation, skin at pad sites.

name: Echocardiogram
shortExplanation: An ultrasound of the heart that shows how well it pumps, how the valves move, and whether there's fluid around it — a painless bedside or lab test.

sections.targetConcern: Need to assess heart function (ejection fraction), valve disease, wall motion after MI, or a pericardial effusion.
sections.whatToMonitor: For a transthoracic study, no special monitoring; for a transesophageal (TEE) study, airway, sedation level, and gag reflex/NPO status before eating.

name: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
shortExplanation: A test that records the brain's electrical activity through scalp electrodes. It is used to diagnose seizures and evaluate altered consciousness.

sections.targetConcern: Detecting abnormal electrical activity to diagnose and classify seizures and epilepsy, evaluate unexplained altered mental status, identify nonconvulsive status epilepticus, and assess brain function; continuous EEG is used in the ICU.
sections.whatToMonitor: Painless and noninvasive. Hair should be clean and free of products; sleep deprivation or photic stimulation may be used to provoke findings. Note any clinical events and their timing during recording. After the study, help remove electrode paste; resume medications per orders.

name: Endotracheal Intubation
shortExplanation: Placement of a breathing tube into the trachea to secure the airway and allow mechanical ventilation — used in respiratory failure or when a patient can't protect their own airway.

sections.targetConcern: Respiratory failure or inability to protect the airway.
sections.whatToMonitor: Tube placement (breath sounds, capnography, chest x-ray), oxygen saturation, blood pressure during and after the procedure, signs of accidental extubation.

name: Enteral Feeding Administration
shortExplanation: Delivering nutrition through a feeding tube, either continuously by pump or as scheduled bolus feeds.

sections.targetConcern: Provides nutrition and hydration to patients who cannot safely eat by mouth but have a working gut, using nasogastric or gastrostomy tubes.
sections.whatToMonitor: Keep the head of bed elevated at least 30-45 degrees during and after feeds to prevent aspiration. Confirm tube placement, check gastric residuals or tolerance per policy, and watch for distension, nausea, and diarrhea. Flush the tube before and after feeds and medications, and monitor blood glucose, electrolytes, and weight; refeeding syndrome is a risk in malnourished patients.

name: Epidural Analgesia
shortExplanation: A regional anesthesia technique in which medication is delivered through a small catheter near the spinal nerves to relieve labor pain.

sections.targetConcern: Provides effective pain relief during labor and delivery while keeping the mother awake, and can be dosed further if a cesarean becomes necessary.
sections.whatToMonitor: Watch for maternal hypotension, which is the most common complication and can reduce placental blood flow, so monitor blood pressure frequently and continue fetal heart rate monitoring. Also assess for urinary retention, degree of motor block and fall risk, itching, fever, and postdural puncture headache. A fluid bolus is often given beforehand to reduce hypotension.

name: Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
shortExplanation: Tracking the baby's heart rate and the mother's contractions during labor to assess how well the fetus is tolerating labor.

sections.targetConcern: Detects signs of fetal hypoxia or distress so the team can intervene before harm occurs, most often using external Doppler and a contraction sensor.
sections.whatToMonitor: Assess baseline rate (normal roughly 110-160 beats per minute), variability, accelerations, and decelerations in relation to contractions. Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency, and variable decelerations suggest cord compression. For nonreassuring patterns, reposition the mother, give IV fluids and oxygen, stop oxytocin, and notify the provider.

name: Foley Catheter Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of an indwelling urinary catheter to drain the bladder and allow accurate output monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Urinary retention, need for precise hourly output monitoring (e.g. in shock or with diuretic therapy), or immobility complicating toileting.
sections.whatToMonitor: Urine color/clarity/amount, signs of catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI), skin integrity around the insertion site, bladder distension if the catheter appears blocked.

name: General Anesthesia
shortExplanation: A medically induced, reversible state of unconsciousness with loss of sensation and reflexes so surgery can be performed. The airway is usually controlled with an endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway.

sections.targetConcern: Allows major or painful surgery by producing unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, and muscle relaxation while the anesthesia team supports breathing and hemodynamics.
sections.whatToMonitor: Airway patency and ventilation, oxygen saturation and end-tidal CO2, blood pressure and heart rate, temperature, and level of consciousness on emergence. Watch for airway obstruction, laryngospasm, hypotension, hypothermia, and postoperative nausea after extubation.

name: Glasgow Coma Scale
shortExplanation: A standardized scale that rates level of consciousness by scoring eye, verbal, and motor responses. It is used to assess and track brain injury severity.

sections.targetConcern: Rapidly and reproducibly assessing level of consciousness after brain injury or acute neurologic change, and tracking trends that signal improvement or deterioration.
sections.whatToMonitor: Scores three components: eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5), and motor response (1 to 6), for a total of 3 to 15. Lower scores indicate deeper impairment; a score of 8 or less generally reflects coma and concern for airway protection. Note the best response and any decline promptly.

name: Hemodialysis
shortExplanation: Filters waste, excess fluid, and electrolytes from the blood using an external machine — used when the kidneys can no longer do this on their own.

sections.targetConcern: Acute kidney injury or end-stage renal disease with dangerous fluid overload, electrolyte imbalance, or uremia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure during treatment (intradialytic hypotension is common), fluid removal amount versus goal, vascular access site (fistula/graft/catheter) patency and infection signs, post-dialysis electrolytes.

name: ICD Placement
shortExplanation: Implantation of a device that continuously watches the heart rhythm and delivers a shock automatically if a life-threatening arrhythmia occurs.

sections.targetConcern: High risk of sudden cardiac death — e.g. survived cardiac arrest, reduced ejection fraction, or dangerous ventricular arrhythmias.
sections.whatToMonitor: Implant pocket for bleeding/hematoma or infection, arm movement restrictions on the implant side, device function and any delivered shocks, signs of lead dislodgement.

name: Lumbar Puncture
shortExplanation: Needle sampling of cerebrospinal fluid from the lower spine — used to diagnose conditions like meningitis or to relieve elevated pressure around the brain.

sections.targetConcern: Suspected CNS infection (e.g. meningitis) or need to measure/relieve elevated intracranial pressure.
sections.whatToMonitor: Post-procedure headache (positional, from CSF leak), neuro checks, insertion site for bleeding or CSF leakage.

name: Moderate Sedation
shortExplanation: Drug-induced depression of consciousness in which the patient responds purposefully to voice or light touch and keeps their own airway and breathing. It is used for procedures such as endoscopy, cardioversion, and line placement.

sections.targetConcern: Provides comfort, anxiolysis, and analgesia for shorter procedures without the airway support and full unconsciousness of general anesthesia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Level of responsiveness, respiratory rate and depth, oxygen saturation, capnography where available, and blood pressure and heart rate. Watch for oversedation and airway obstruction; have oxygen, suction, and reversal agents (naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines) immediately available.

name: Nasogastric Tube Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of a tube through the nose into the stomach for gastric decompression, medication delivery, or short-term enteral feeding.

sections.targetConcern: Bowel obstruction requiring decompression, inability to take oral intake, or need for short-term enteral nutrition/medication access.
sections.whatToMonitor: Placement confirmation (x-ray and/or aspirate pH), drainage amount/color, nasal and throat skin integrity, aspiration risk during feeds.

name: NIH Stroke Scale
shortExplanation: A standardized 15-item neurologic exam that quantifies stroke severity and guides treatment decisions and monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Objectively measuring the severity of neurologic deficits in acute stroke to guide thrombolysis and thrombectomy decisions, track changes over time, and communicate status among the care team.
sections.whatToMonitor: Assesses level of consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, motor arm and leg strength, limb ataxia, sensation, language, speech (dysarthria), and inattention. Higher total scores indicate more severe strokes. Repeat serially to detect improvement or deterioration.

name: Oropharyngeal and Nasotracheal Suctioning
shortExplanation: Using a suction catheter to clear secretions from the mouth, throat, or airway in patients who cannot clear them on their own.

sections.targetConcern: Removes secretions to maintain a patent airway, improve oxygenation, and reduce aspiration and infection risk in patients with a weak cough or excessive secretions.
sections.whatToMonitor: Pre-oxygenate and limit each pass to about 10-15 seconds; apply suction only while withdrawing. Watch oxygen saturation, heart rate, and rhythm - suctioning can cause hypoxia, vagal-mediated bradycardia, and mucosal trauma. Stop and reoxygenate for desaturation or arrhythmia, and note secretion color and amount.

name: Ostomy Care
shortExplanation: The care of a surgical stoma that diverts stool or urine into an external pouch, including skin protection and output monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Manages a colostomy, ileostomy, or urostomy - a surgically created opening (stoma) that routes waste into an external appliance.
sections.whatToMonitor: A healthy stoma is pink to red and moist; report a dusky, pale, or black stoma immediately. Protect the surrounding (peristomal) skin, ensure a good pouch seal, and monitor output, since high-volume ileostomy output can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.

name: Pacemaker Insertion
shortExplanation: Implantation of a small device under the skin with leads into the heart that deliver electrical impulses to keep the heart beating at an adequate rate.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade heart block, or another conduction problem where the heart's own rate is too slow to meet the body's needs.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion pocket for bleeding/hematoma or infection, heart rate and rhythm to confirm capture, arm movement restrictions on the implant side, signs of lead dislodgement (hiccups, failure to pace).

name: Packed Red Blood Cell Transfusion
shortExplanation: Infusion of donor red blood cells to treat significant blood loss or anemia that's causing symptoms or instability.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic anemia or acute blood loss where the patient's own red cell count is too low to meet oxygen delivery needs.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs closely (especially the first 15 minutes), signs of transfusion reaction (fever, chills, rash, back pain, dyspnea) — stop the transfusion immediately and notify the provider if suspected.

name: Paracentesis
shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the abdominal cavity — relieves pressure from ascites and can help identify its cause.

sections.targetConcern: Large-volume ascites causing abdominal distension, discomfort, or respiratory compromise; or ascites of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs for hypotension from fluid shifts (especially with large-volume taps), insertion site for leakage, need for albumin replacement after large-volume removal.

name: PEG Tube Placement
shortExplanation: Endoscopic placement of a feeding tube directly through the abdominal wall into the stomach — used when a patient needs long-term enteral nutrition.

sections.targetConcern: Inability to safely swallow or take adequate oral nutrition long-term (e.g. after stroke, in progressive neurologic disease).
sections.whatToMonitor: Stoma site for infection/leakage, tube placement before each feed, feeding tolerance (nausea, distension), skin integrity around the site.

name: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
shortExplanation: Threading a catheter through an artery to open a blocked coronary vessel — a balloon widens the narrowing and a stent is usually left behind to hold it open, restoring blood flow to the heart.

sections.targetConcern: A blocked or critically narrowed coronary artery, most urgently in an acute heart attack (STEMI) where fast reperfusion limits heart muscle damage.
sections.whatToMonitor: Access site (radial/femoral) for bleeding or hematoma, distal pulses of the cannulated limb, chest pain and ECG changes (possible re-occlusion or stent thrombosis), renal function after contrast dye.

name: Pericardiocentesis
shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the sac around the heart — relieves pressure that keeps the heart from filling and pumping, most urgently in cardiac tamponade.

sections.targetConcern: Pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins), or an effusion of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure and heart rate for rapid improvement or re-accumulation, ECG changes, insertion site for bleeding, signs of recurring tamponade.

name: Peripheral IV Insertion
shortExplanation: Placing a short catheter into a peripheral vein, usually in the arm or hand, for fluids and medications.

sections.targetConcern: Establishes venous access to give IV fluids, medications, contrast, and blood products, and to draw blood at insertion.
sections.whatToMonitor: After insertion, check the site regularly for infiltration (swelling, coolness), extravasation of vesicants, phlebitis (redness, pain, a cordlike vein), and signs of infection. Ensure a brisk flush and blood return, secure the catheter and date the dressing, and rotate sites per policy.

name: Peritoneal Dialysis
shortExplanation: A home-capable form of dialysis that uses the lining of the abdomen (peritoneum) as a natural filter to remove wastes and fluid.

sections.targetConcern: Removes waste products and excess fluid in kidney failure by instilling dialysate into the abdomen, letting it dwell, and draining it.
sections.whatToMonitor: Cloudy drained fluid (effluent), which signals peritonitis; catheter exit-site infection; fluid balance and daily weights; dwell and drain volumes; and blood glucose, since the dialysate contains dextrose.

name: Phototherapy
shortExplanation: Treatment that uses special blue light to lower a newborn's bilirubin level and clear jaundice.

sections.targetConcern: Reduces elevated bilirubin by converting it into water-soluble forms the baby can excrete, preventing progression to brain injury.
sections.whatToMonitor: Protect the infant's eyes with shielding and expose as much skin as possible for maximum light exposure. Monitor temperature (both overheating and cooling can occur), hydration and urine output, feeding, and skin integrity. Track bilirubin levels to gauge response, and watch for loose stools and rash as expected effects.

name: PICC Line Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of a long catheter through an arm vein that terminates near the heart — used for extended IV access without repeated peripheral sticks.

sections.targetConcern: Need for extended IV access, e.g. multi-week antibiotic courses or medications that irritate peripheral veins.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion site for infection/phlebitis, arm swelling or pain (possible thrombosis), catheter tip position confirmed by x-ray.

name: Pulmonary Function Test (PFT)
shortExplanation: A set of breathing tests, usually spirometry, that measure lung volumes and airflow to diagnose and classify lung disease.

sections.targetConcern: Diagnoses and monitors obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) versus restrictive disease by measuring values such as FEV1, FVC, and the FEV1/FVC ratio; often repeated after a bronchodilator to assess reversibility.
sections.whatToMonitor: During testing watch for dizziness, lightheadedness, or bronchospasm from repeated forced breathing. Hold short-acting bronchodilators before the test if reversibility is being assessed and per protocol. Ensure the patient is rested afterward and reassess respiratory status.

name: Radiation Therapy
shortExplanation: The use of high-energy radiation to destroy or shrink cancer cells in a targeted area of the body. It can be curative, given with chemotherapy, or used to relieve symptoms such as pain.

sections.targetConcern: Damages the DNA of cancer cells in the treated field so they cannot grow and divide, while sparing surrounding tissue as much as possible; it is often given as a series of daily treatments.
sections.whatToMonitor: Site-specific effects depending on the area treated, such as skin redness and breakdown in the field, fatigue, mucositis and difficulty swallowing with head, neck, or chest treatment, diarrhea with abdominal or pelvic treatment, and low blood counts. Provide gentle skin care in the treated area, protect it from sun and irritation, and manage fatigue and local symptoms.

name: Rapid Sequence Intubation
shortExplanation: A rapid method to secure the airway by giving a sedative and a paralytic almost simultaneously, then placing a breathing tube, used in emergencies to reduce the risk of aspiration.

sections.targetConcern: Quickly and safely securing a definitive airway in patients who need intubation but are at risk of vomiting and aspiration, such as those with full stomachs, trauma, or respiratory failure.
sections.whatToMonitor: Continuous pulse oximetry and waveform capnography to confirm tube placement, heart rate and blood pressure, and end-tidal CO2. After placement, confirm tube position, secure the tube, monitor ventilation and sedation, and obtain a chest X-ray to verify depth.

name: Spinal Anesthesia
shortExplanation: A single injection of local anesthetic into the cerebrospinal fluid of the lower back that numbs the lower body for surgery. It is common for cesarean sections, and lower-abdominal, pelvic, and lower-extremity procedures.

sections.targetConcern: Provides dense sensory and motor block below the injection level so surgery can be done without general anesthesia, letting the patient stay awake or lightly sedated.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure closely (sympathetic blockade causes hypotension and bradycardia), block level, respiratory effort if the block rises too high, urinary retention, and return of motor/sensory function. Watch for post-dural-puncture headache in the days afterward.

name: Synchronized Cardioversion
shortExplanation: A timed electrical shock delivered to reset an abnormal heart rhythm back to a normal pattern — used when a fast, unstable rhythm needs to be corrected quickly.

sections.targetConcern: Unstable or persistent symptomatic tachyarrhythmia, commonly atrial fibrillation, that hasn't responded to (or can't wait for) medication alone.
sections.whatToMonitor: Rhythm and pulse immediately before/after, sedation level and airway, skin at pad placement sites, blood pressure.

name: Targeted Temperature Management
shortExplanation: Deliberately controlling a patient's body temperature (often after cardiac arrest) to protect the brain and prevent fever.

sections.targetConcern: Reducing brain injury and improving neurologic outcomes in comatose survivors of cardiac arrest by maintaining a controlled target temperature and preventing fever.
sections.whatToMonitor: Core temperature via a reliable probe (bladder, esophageal, or blood), continuous cardiac rhythm, blood pressure, and neuro exam. Watch for shivering, bradycardia, electrolyte shifts (potassium, magnesium), hyperglycemia, and coagulopathy. Rewarm slowly and avoid rebound fever.

name: TAVR
shortExplanation: A minimally invasive procedure that replaces a narrowed aortic valve without open-heart surgery.

sections.targetConcern: Severe aortic stenosis in patients who are poor candidates for open surgical valve replacement.
sections.whatToMonitor: Access site for bleeding/hematoma, rhythm changes, blood pressure, signs of stroke.

name: Thoracentesis
shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the space around the lung — done to relieve breathing difficulty or to diagnose the cause of a pleural effusion.

sections.targetConcern: Pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise, or an effusion of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Respiratory status during and after the procedure, signs of pneumothorax (sudden dyspnea, decreased breath sounds), insertion site for bleeding.

name: Tracheostomy
shortExplanation: Surgical creation of an airway opening in the neck directly into the trachea — used when a patient needs prolonged mechanical ventilation or has an upper airway obstruction.

sections.targetConcern: Anticipated prolonged mechanical ventilation, or upper airway obstruction that an endotracheal tube can't safely address long-term.
sections.whatToMonitor: Stoma site for bleeding/infection, cuff pressure, secretion volume and suctioning needs, signs of accidental decannulation.

name: Upper Endoscopy (EGD)
shortExplanation: A procedure using a flexible scope to view the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. Used to diagnose and treat problems such as ulcers, bleeding, and reflux damage.

sections.targetConcern: Evaluates upper GI symptoms and bleeding, ulcers, varices, strictures, tumors, and reflux injury; allows biopsy, band ligation of varices, cautery of bleeding, and dilation of strictures.
sections.whatToMonitor: After the procedure, monitor level of consciousness and vital signs as sedation wears off, and confirm the gag reflex has returned before giving food or fluids. Watch for signs of perforation or bleeding: severe abdominal or chest pain, fever, difficulty swallowing, hematemesis, or melena.

name: Venipuncture (Blood Draw)
shortExplanation: Puncturing a vein with a needle to collect blood samples for laboratory testing.

sections.targetConcern: Obtains venous blood for diagnostic testing. Correct technique and tube handling protect the accuracy of results.
sections.whatToMonitor: Draw tubes in the correct order and fill to volume; mix additive tubes gently to avoid clots or hemolysis. Avoid drawing above an IV or from the arm with a fistula or on the mastectomy side. After removal, hold pressure and check for hematoma; watch for lightheadedness or fainting in anxious patients. Label tubes at the bedside.

name: Wound Culture Collection
shortExplanation: Sampling a wound to identify infecting organisms and guide antibiotic therapy.

sections.targetConcern: Identifies the organisms causing a wound infection and their antibiotic sensitivities in cellulitis, surgical-site infection, or a non-healing ulcer.
sections.whatToMonitor: Cleanse the wound with saline first so you sample infected tissue, not surface colonizers; the Levine technique (rotating a swab over viable tissue) is preferred, and deep tissue or aspirate is best. Note wound appearance, drainage, and odor. Collect before starting antibiotics when feasible, and follow up on culture results and healing.

name: Wound Debridement
shortExplanation: The removal of dead, damaged, or infected tissue from a wound to promote healing.

sections.targetConcern: Removes nonviable tissue (slough and eschar) and debris that block healing and harbor infection, converting a chronic wound toward a healing state.
sections.whatToMonitor: Assess for bleeding and pain during and after the procedure, signs of infection, and the appearance of healthy granulation tissue. Methods include sharp/surgical, enzymatic, autolytic (moist dressings), and mechanical debridement.

name: ACLS Cardiac Arrest Algorithm
shortExplanation: The standardized team response to cardiac arrest — high-quality CPR, rhythm checks, shocks for shockable rhythms, and timed medications.

sections.triggerCriteria: Pulseless patient — confirmed cardiac arrest. Rhythm sorted into shockable (VF/pulseless VT) or non-shockable (asystole/PEA).
sections.steps: Start high-quality CPR and attach the monitor/defibrillator. Shockable: defibrillate, resume CPR, give epinephrine every 3–5 min, add amiodarone, shock with each rhythm check. Non-shockable: CPR with epinephrine every 3–5 min. Throughout, search for and treat reversible causes (the Hs and Ts) and minimize interruptions in compressions.

name: Advance Directives
shortExplanation: Legal documents that let people state their wishes for medical care if they become unable to speak for themselves. They include living wills and the naming of a healthcare decision-maker.

sections.triggerCriteria: Relevant to all adults, and especially important for patients with serious or terminal illness. They guide care when a patient loses the capacity to make or communicate decisions.
sections.steps: Key forms include a living will (preferences for treatments such as CPR, intubation, and artificial nutrition), a durable power of attorney for healthcare or healthcare proxy (naming a surrogate decision-maker), and portable medical orders such as POLST/MOLST that translate wishes into actionable clinician orders. Nurses confirm documents are on the chart and honored, clarify code status, help patients and families discuss goals, and ensure directives are communicated across care transitions.

name: Cancer Pain Management
shortExplanation: A structured approach to relieving pain in cancer patients, often guided by the WHO analgesic ladder. It combines scheduled and as-needed medications with attention to side effects and quality of life.

sections.triggerCriteria: Applies to patients with cancer-related pain from the tumor, treatment, or procedures. Pain is assessed regularly with a consistent scale and characterized by type (for example nociceptive versus neuropathic) to guide therapy.
sections.steps: Match analgesia to pain severity along the WHO ladder: non-opioids such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs for mild pain, adding opioids as pain increases, plus adjuvants (for example agents for neuropathic pain) at any step. Use around-the-clock dosing for constant pain with breakthrough doses available, prevent opioid-induced constipation with a proactive bowel regimen, and monitor for sedation and respiratory depression. Reassess response frequently and involve palliative care for complex pain.

name: Chest Pain Protocol
shortExplanation: A standardized first response to new chest pain to quickly identify or rule out a heart attack.

sections.triggerCriteria: New or ongoing chest pain or an anginal equivalent (e.g. unexplained dyspnea, especially in higher-risk patients).
sections.steps: Get a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, draw troponin (trended serially), apply continuous cardiac monitoring, establish IV access, and consider the initial "MONA" measures — aspirin, nitroglycerin, oxygen if hypoxic, and pain control — while escalating to the STEMI pathway if ECG shows ST elevation.

name: CIWA-Ar Protocol
shortExplanation: A standardized scale used to measure the severity of alcohol withdrawal and guide how much benzodiazepine to give.

sections.triggerCriteria: Used for patients at risk of or experiencing alcohol withdrawal, typically those with a history of heavy alcohol use who have stopped or reduced drinking. It is applied on a schedule and whenever withdrawal symptoms appear.
sections.steps: Score ten items: nausea and vomiting, tremor, paroxysmal sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile disturbances, auditory disturbances, visual disturbances, headache, and orientation/clouding of sensorium. Sum the items; higher totals indicate more severe withdrawal. Use the score to drive symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing per the order set, reassess at set intervals, and escalate care for high or rising scores. Ensure thiamine, fluids, and a safe environment alongside scoring.

name: Discharge Planning
shortExplanation: The process of preparing a patient to leave the hospital safely and arranging the care and resources they will need afterward. Good discharge planning reduces complications and avoidable readmissions.

sections.triggerCriteria: Begins early in the hospital stay, ideally at admission, for all patients and is intensified for those with complex needs, limited support, or high readmission risk.
sections.steps: Assess the patient's functional status, home situation, support system, and post-discharge needs; determine the appropriate next level of care (home, home health, or a facility); reconcile medications and arrange prescriptions and equipment; schedule follow-up appointments and any home services; and provide clear, teach-back-verified education on medications, warning signs, and self-care. Confirm transportation and communicate the plan to the patient, family, and receiving providers.

name: Hospice Care
shortExplanation: A model of care focused on comfort and quality of life for people near the end of life who are no longer seeking curative treatment. An interdisciplinary team supports the patient and family, often at home.

sections.triggerCriteria: Generally for patients with a terminal illness and a life expectancy of about six months or less if the disease follows its usual course, who choose comfort-focused care over curative treatment. Eligibility is periodically recertified.
sections.steps: An interdisciplinary team (nurse, physician, aide, social worker, chaplain, and volunteers) manages symptoms such as pain, dyspnea, nausea, and agitation, and supports psychosocial and spiritual needs. Care emphasizes comfort measures, advance care planning, medication and equipment for the home, caregiver teaching and respite, and bereavement support for the family after death.

name: Isolation Precautions
shortExplanation: A tiered set of infection-control practices used to prevent the spread of infectious agents in healthcare, built on standard precautions plus transmission-based precautions.

sections.triggerCriteria: Standard precautions apply to all patients at all times. Transmission-based precautions are added when a patient is known or suspected to be infected or colonized with an organism spread by contact, droplet, or airborne routes (for example MRSA or C. difficile for contact, influenza for droplet, and tuberculosis, measles, or varicella for airborne).
sections.steps: Standard precautions: hand hygiene, gloves and other PPE based on anticipated exposure, safe injection practices, and respiratory hygiene. Contact: gown and gloves; dedicated or disinfected equipment; note that C. difficile and other spores require soap-and-water handwashing. Droplet: surgical mask within about 6 feet and a private room when possible. Airborne: an N95 or higher respirator and a negative-pressure (airborne infection isolation) room with the door closed. Educate patients and visitors, and don and doff PPE correctly to avoid self-contamination.

name: Neutropenic Precautions
shortExplanation: Protective measures used to reduce infection exposure in patients with very low neutrophil counts. The goal is to shield an immunocompromised patient from avoidable germs.

sections.triggerCriteria: Initiated for patients with significant neutropenia (for example an ANC below 500, or a falling count expected to reach that range), most often during chemotherapy or after transplant.
sections.steps: Strict hand hygiene by everyone entering the room, a private room, and screening out visitors and staff who are ill. Avoid fresh flowers and standing water, follow food-safety practices, provide meticulous skin, oral, and perineal care, and minimize invasive procedures. Monitor temperature closely and report any fever immediately, since fever may be the only sign of a life-threatening infection.

name: Palliative Care
shortExplanation: Specialized care focused on relieving the symptoms and stress of a serious illness and improving quality of life. Unlike hospice, it can be given at any stage of illness and alongside curative or life-prolonging treatment.

sections.triggerCriteria: Appropriate for any patient with a serious illness (such as cancer, heart failure, COPD, or advanced kidney disease), at any stage and any age, regardless of whether they are also pursuing curative treatment.
sections.steps: An interdisciplinary team assesses and manages distressing symptoms (pain, dyspnea, nausea, fatigue, anxiety), clarifies goals of care and prognosis, supports complex decision-making and advance care planning, and coordinates care across settings. Nurses reassess symptoms frequently, support the patient and family emotionally, and help transition to hospice when appropriate.

name: Perioperative VTE Prophylaxis
shortExplanation: Measures used around surgery to prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, since surgery and immobility raise clotting risk. It combines mechanical and, when appropriate, pharmacologic methods.

sections.triggerCriteria: Assess every surgical patient for clot risk (for example with a Caprini score) and balance it against bleeding risk. Higher risk comes with major or orthopedic surgery, cancer, prolonged immobility, prior VTE, obesity, and advanced age.
sections.steps: Mechanical prophylaxis such as sequential compression devices and early ambulation for most patients, with pharmacologic prophylaxis (low-dose heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin) added when bleeding risk allows. Ensure compression devices are worn and functioning, encourage early mobilization, monitor for signs of DVT (unilateral leg swelling and pain) and PE (sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxia), and reassess as bleeding risk changes.

name: Post-Acute Care Levels
shortExplanation: The different settings a patient may go to after a hospital stay, ranging from home with services to specialized facilities. Choosing the right level matches the patient's care needs with the appropriate intensity of services.

sections.triggerCriteria: Considered during discharge planning when a patient cannot safely go straight home or needs ongoing skilled care, rehabilitation, or supervision.
sections.steps: Common options, from lower to higher intensity, include home with home health services (intermittent skilled nursing and therapy), skilled nursing facility (SNF) for short-term rehab and skilled care, inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) for intensive daily therapy in patients who can tolerate it, and long-term acute care hospital (LTACH) for medically complex patients needing extended hospital-level care. Match the setting to the patient's medical and functional needs and therapy tolerance, verify insurance coverage and qualifying criteria, and coordinate the transfer and records.

name: Preoperative Fasting (NPO)
shortExplanation: Withholding food and drink for a set time before anesthesia to reduce the risk of stomach contents being aspirated into the lungs. It is often shortened to NPO, meaning nothing by mouth.

sections.triggerCriteria: Applies to patients scheduled for anesthesia or sedation. Standard minimum fasting times for healthy patients are about 2 hours for clear liquids, 6 hours for a light meal or non-human milk, and 8 hours or more for fried or fatty foods and full meals.
sections.steps: Confirm and document the last oral intake, clarify NPO status with the anesthesia team, and hold or clarify oral medications per orders (many are taken with a sip of water). Encourage clear fluids up to the allowed window to avoid unnecessary dehydration, verify NPO before transport, and reassess if surgery is delayed. Watch for aspiration risk in emergencies, pregnancy, obesity, diabetes with gastroparesis, and bowel obstruction.

name: Prior Authorization
shortExplanation: A requirement by an insurer to approve a medication, test, procedure, or level of care before it will be covered. Delays in authorization can hold up treatment and discharge.

sections.triggerCriteria: Required by many insurance plans for certain high-cost drugs, imaging, procedures, durable medical equipment, and post-acute placements before the service is delivered or covered.
sections.steps: Identify services that need authorization early, submit the clinical documentation supporting medical necessity, and track the request to approval or denial. If denied, pursue peer-to-peer review or appeal, or arrange a covered alternative. Case managers coordinate with providers, pharmacy, and the payer, communicate expected timelines, and work to prevent authorization delays from postponing care or discharge.

name: Rapid Response Team
shortExplanation: A dedicated team called to the bedside when a patient shows early signs of deterioration, aiming to intervene before a full cardiac or respiratory arrest.

sections.triggerCriteria: Acute changes in vital signs or condition, such as a marked rise or fall in heart rate, respiratory rate, or blood pressure, falling oxygen saturation, new altered mental status, decreased urine output, or simply staff or family concern that the patient is deteriorating.
sections.steps: Any staff member activates the team. The responders (often ICU nurse, respiratory therapist, and provider) rapidly assess airway, breathing, circulation, and mental status, begin interventions such as oxygen, fluids, or medications, order labs and imaging, and decide on escalation - including transfer to a higher level of care - while communicating with the primary team.

name: RASS Sedation Scale
shortExplanation: A standardized scale used to rate a patient's level of agitation or sedation, helping teams titrate sedatives to a target rather than over- or under-sedating.

sections.triggerCriteria: Used for any patient receiving sedation, particularly mechanically ventilated ICU patients, to set and reassess a sedation goal and to detect agitation or over-sedation.
sections.steps: Score the patient from +4 (combative) through 0 (alert and calm) to -5 (unarousable), based on observed behavior and response to voice then physical stimulation. Compare the current score with the ordered target, then titrate sedation up or down to reach the goal. Reassess regularly, and pair with lighter sedation and daily awakening and breathing trials when appropriate.

name: Readmission Risk Reduction
shortExplanation: Efforts to identify patients likely to return to the hospital soon after discharge and to prevent it. Reducing avoidable readmissions improves outcomes and lowers costs.

sections.triggerCriteria: Screen patients for readmission risk during the admission. Higher-risk features include multiple chronic conditions, prior recent admissions, polypharmacy, older age, mental health or substance use issues, limited health literacy or social support, and unstable housing or finances.
sections.steps: Target high-risk patients with enhanced interventions: careful medication reconciliation, clear teach-back education on the condition and warning signs, timely follow-up appointments, follow-up phone calls after discharge, connection to home health or community resources, and attention to social barriers such as transportation and medication cost. Ensure a warm handoff to outpatient and post-acute providers so nothing falls through the cracks.

name: Sepsis Bundle
shortExplanation: A standardized set of time-sensitive actions performed when sepsis is suspected, designed to improve survival by acting quickly.

sections.triggerCriteria: Suspected infection plus signs of organ dysfunction or meeting systemic inflammatory criteria, per unit/hospital sepsis screening tool.
sections.steps: Draw blood cultures before antibiotics, measure lactate, start broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, begin IV fluid resuscitation, reassess and add vasopressors if hypotension persists after fluids.

name: Sliding-Scale Insulin
shortExplanation: An ordered plan in which the dose of rapid- or short-acting insulin increases as the measured blood glucose rises.

sections.triggerCriteria: Scheduled blood glucose checks (commonly before meals and at bedtime) that map to a prescribed insulin dose, with larger doses at higher glucose values.
sections.steps: Check glucose at the ordered times, give the corresponding insulin dose per the order, treat and recheck for hypoglycemia if low, and document. It is usually paired with scheduled basal insulin; reactive sliding scale alone is discouraged for ongoing diabetes control.

name: Social Determinants of Health
shortExplanation: The non-medical conditions in which people live and work that strongly influence their health, such as housing, food, income, and access to care. Addressing them is central to case management and reducing readmissions.

sections.triggerCriteria: Screen all patients, and especially those with frequent admissions, poor disease control, or complex social situations, for unmet social needs that could undermine their care plan.
sections.steps: Key domains include economic stability, housing and neighborhood safety, food security, education and health literacy, transportation, and access to health care and social support. Use a screening tool to identify needs, then connect patients to resources such as financial assistance, medication and food programs, transportation, home services, and community organizations. Tailor discharge plans to real-world barriers and document and communicate needs so the care team can follow up.

name: Spontaneous Breathing Trial
shortExplanation: A test of whether a ventilated patient can breathe on their own with minimal support, used to decide readiness for removing the breathing tube.

sections.triggerCriteria: Considered when the reason for intubation is improving, oxygenation is adequate on low support, the patient is hemodynamically stable with minimal or no vasopressors, is able to initiate breaths, and often after a sedation pause (spontaneous awakening trial).
sections.steps: Reduce ventilator support to a minimal level (such as low pressure support or a T-piece) and observe the patient breathing on their own for roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours. Watch respiratory rate, tidal volume, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, and work of breathing or distress. If the patient tolerates it, proceed toward extubation; if they fail, resume full support and reassess the causes.

name: STEMI Protocol
shortExplanation: A time-critical pathway to reopen a blocked coronary artery fast in a full-thickness heart attack — "time is muscle."

sections.triggerCriteria: ST-elevation on a 12-lead ECG with ischemic symptoms — activates the cath lab immediately.
sections.steps: Obtain a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival, activate the cath lab, give aspirin and a second antiplatelet plus anticoagulation, manage pain/ischemia, and get the patient to PCI with a door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes (fibrinolytics if timely PCI isn't available).

name: Suicidal Ideation and Safety Precautions
shortExplanation: The nursing approach to assessing and protecting a patient who is having thoughts of suicide.

sections.triggerCriteria: A patient expresses thoughts of death or suicide, has a plan or intent, has a history of attempts, or screens positive on a suicide risk screening tool. Sudden calm after distress can also be a warning sign.
sections.steps: Ask directly and nonjudgmentally about thoughts, plan, intent, and access to means. Place the patient on the appropriate level of observation (up to one-to-one continuous observation) and remove dangerous items from the environment. Maintain a safe, searched room, document risk assessment and interventions, communicate risk at handoff, and involve the mental health team. Provide a supportive, nonjudgmental presence and reassess risk regularly.

name: Surgical Safety Checklist
shortExplanation: A standardized team checklist used before, during, and after an operation to prevent avoidable harm such as wrong-site surgery. The surgical time-out is its central pause.

sections.triggerCriteria: Performed for every operative procedure, at three points: sign-in before anesthesia induction, time-out before skin incision, and sign-out before the patient leaves the room.
sections.steps: Sign-in: confirm patient identity, procedure, site marking, consent, allergies, and airway/aspiration risk. Time-out: the whole team pauses to confirm correct patient, procedure, and site, review anticipated critical events, and confirm antibiotic prophylaxis and imaging. Sign-out: confirm the procedure performed, correct instrument, sponge, and needle counts, specimen labeling, and equipment issues, and review recovery concerns.
